When what is sent will not fit, the answer says so rather than losing the start of it.
    • Installed: each model with its size and what it can do: tools (can read and edit files), no tools (sees only what is sent), thinks, loaded (in memory now). Use picks it for the pane (the model menu in the pane does too); the bin deletes it from the server, after a second click.
    • Add a model: any name from the Ollama library (qwen3:8b, gpt-oss:20b), or one of the suggestions. Downloads run on the server, so closing the page does not stop one; each shows its progress and can be stopped. A model needs roughly its size in free memory to run.

    Installing, starting, stopping and changing models are for an administrator of the server (anyone, with noAuth); everyone can pick among the models.

    server:
  assistant:
    ollama:
      enabled: true              # off until this is set
      model: qwen3:8b            # the default, if installed (else the first one)
      contextLength: 16384       # tokens; also OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH for an Ollama orgs starts
      url: http://127.0.0.1:11434   # another machine's Ollama works too (orgs only starts a local one)
      serve: true                # start ollama serve when nothing answers
      download: true             # allow Install Ollama from worg
      command: ""                # the ollama binary, if not on the PATH or in Ollama.app
      modelDir: ""               # where models are kept (default ~/.ollama/models)
      keepAlive: 30m             # how long a model stays loaded after a question
      think: false               # thinking on or off for models that can (unset: the model's default)

    Nothing is sent until you ask. The conversation is about this file and goes when you open another.

    On the server (keys never reach the browser):

    server:
  assistant:
    backend: claude              # the default; "off" turns the assistant off for everyone
    claude:
      apiKey: "keyring:anthropic"   # or "env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", or the key itself
      model: claude-opus-5-5
      models: [claude-sonnet-5-5]   # others to offer
      effort: medium                # low, medium, high, xhigh, max
    chatgpt:
      apiKey: "env:OPENAI_API_KEY"
      model: gpt-5
      url: ""                       # an OpenAI-compatible server (a local model) instead
    gemini:
      apiKey: "env:GEMINI_API_KEY"
      model: gemini-flash-latest

    With no apiKey each backend reads its usual environment variable, and Claude also an ant auth login profile. disabled: true hides one backend.

    LanguageTool

    LanguageTool is a real spelling, grammar and style checker. Switch it on in the menu by Check (▾) and it does all three; the built-in rules stand in for a paragraph until its answer comes. The menu has:

    • Server: the orgs server's own (one orgs runs for you, set up in orgs.yaml, below; your text goes to orgs and no further), public (api.languagetool.org, free, with limits), premium (api.languagetoolplus.com, with your user name and API key), or another server by its url (http://localhost:8081). The public and premium servers are sent each paragraph you check. Test sends one sentence and says what answered, in what language, and how fast.
    • Language: detect it (the default, steered by the preferred varieties, en-US unless you say en-GB), one from the list, or any code.
    • Mother tongue: finds false friends for a writer whose first language it is.
    • Picky: LanguageTool's stricter rules for style, tone and wordiness.
    • Check as I type: off, paragraphs are only sent when you press F7.
    • Rules and categories: rule and category ids to switch on or off. Ignore this rule on a problem's fixes adds its rule to the ones switched off.

    Add to dictionary works on LanguageTool's misspellings too: your words are never marked, whoever checks.

    To have orgs run LanguageTool, add to orgs.yaml either an unzipped LanguageTool (LanguageTool-stable.zip, which needs java 17 or later):

    server:
  languageTool:
    enabled: true
    path: "~/tools/LanguageTool-6.6"   # the folder holding languagetool-server.jar

    or, with no path, docker (the erikvl87/languagetool image unless docker: names another). It listens on port 8082 (port:); one already running there is used rather than started again, and orgs stops the one it started when it stops. ngrams: names LanguageTool's n-gram data for the their/there kind of mistake, javaArgs: ["-Xmx2g"] gives it more memory, and url: instead of enabled: passes the checks on to a LanguageTool somebody else runs.

    Keys What it does
    F7 the next problem, with its fixes
    S-F7 thesaurus: synonyms for the word at the cursor
    F8 typewriter on or off (in the plain editor too)
    ]s [s (vim) next, previous problem
    z= (vim), M-$ (emacs) fixes for the word at the cursor
    SPC y (vim), C-c y (emacs) thesaurus

    In a list of fixes or synonyms: the arrows or 1-9, Enter to take one, Esc to put it away. The thesaurus works anywhere in the editor, writing mode or not. It asks datamuse.com, sending only the word looked up. Spelling uses an English (US) dictionary inside the page.

    More optional packages: canvases, trackers, related notes, drawings, media notes, callouts, backlink counts, maps, timelines, a library, hover previews, link titles, maths typing, local pictures

    Turning them on

    These do in orgs what well-loved note-taking plugins do elsewhere, kept in org's own forms - links, properties, keywords and blocks - or, for canvases and drawings, in open file formats other tools read too, linked from org. Like the org packages (see Optional org packages), each is off until it is turned on and does nothing at all while off.

    orgs features                  # which are on
orgs features canvas on        # turn one on; written into the server's yaml

    worg's Org packages… setting and VS Code's Org: Turn orgs Features On or Off list them too.

    server:
  features:
    canvas: true
    tracker: true
    related: true
    excalidraw: true
    mediaNotes: true
    callouts: true
    backlinkCounts: true
    mapView: true
    timeline: true
    mediaDb: true
    hoverEditor: true
    autoLinkTitle: true
    latexSuite: true
    localImages: true

    Canvases (JSON Canvas)

    A canvas is a board of cards and arrows: headings from your org files, notes, pictures and links, laid out on a page with no edges, grouped and joined up. It is kept in a .canvas file beside your org files, in the open JSON Canvas 1.0 format, so the same board opens in other JSON Canvas apps and here. Turn it on with orgs features canvas on.

    What a board is made of
    • Heading cards show an org heading: its keyword, title, tags and text, rendered the way the file view renders it. Opening one (double click) opens the heading.
    • File cards show a whole org file (its title, the start of it, its top headings), a picture, or any other file.
    • Link cards show a web address.
    • Text cards hold a note typed on the board.
    • Groups are labelled boxes around cards; a group moves with the cards in it.
    • Edges join two cards, from a side of one to a side of the other, with an arrow at either end, both or neither, a label and a colour.

    Cards and groups take one of six colours (red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, purple - the 1 to 6 of the format) or any #hex colour.

    How a heading is named in the file

    A heading on a board is a file node naming the org file, with the heading's :ID: as its subpath:

    {"id":"0ba6ef0e2a6b0a3d","type":"file","file":"notes/plans.org","subpath":"#^5f0c2b7e-1d1a-4a65-9f4b-3c2d1e0f9a8b",
 "x":140,"y":-220,"width":400,"height":300}

    When a heading is put on a board it is given an :ID: (in its property drawer, as org-id would) if it has none, so the card keeps finding it when it is renamed or refiled into another file - the board then names the new file on its next save. A heading with a :CUSTOM_ID: and no :ID: is named by its CUSTOM_ID.

    These are read too, for boards made by hand or in other apps:

    Written Finds
    "subpath": "#^ID" the heading with that :ID: (or CUSTOM_ID)
    "subpath": "#Plans#Next year" the heading by its outline path
    "subpath": "#id:ID" an org id: target
    "file": "plans.org::*Plans" org's search option: a heading by title
    "file": "plans.org::#plans" a CUSTOM_ID
    "file": "plans.org::42" the heading line 42 is in

    Paths are relative to the org directory the board is in (vault-relative paths), and are looked for beside the board as well. A heading or file that is not there any more is drawn as a dashed card saying so; nothing is removed.

    Text cards: org or markdown

    In JSON Canvas a text card is markdown. Here a text card is shown as org, unless it reads as markdown and not as org (a # heading, **bold**, [text](url), a ```` ``` ```` fence, a > quote), in which case it is converted to org first. Either way it is written back exactly as you typed it, so a board shared with another app keeps its markdown and a board of your own can be pure org.

    In an org file

    Link to a board the way you link to any file:

    The plan, as it stands: [[file:boards/plan.canvas][The plan board]]

    While the feature is on, the html export (and so worg's rendered view of the file) draws the board itself in its place - groups, cards with their keyword, tags and the start of their text, pictures, arrows and labels - as a picture, with the link's description under it. A board that points at a heading also counts as a link to it: it shows in the heading's backlinks, in HasBacklinks(), and in the link graph.

    In worg

    The Canvas tab (in the sidebar while the feature is on) picks a board or makes a new one, and draws it on a board you can pan (drag the empty board, or scroll) and zoom (ctrl-scroll, pinch, or the buttons; the last button shows everything).

    • Add a heading from the Add a heading… box, a text card, a group, a link or a file from the buttons. A url or text dropped on the board becomes a card where it is dropped; so does a task dragged from the day planner's list.
    • Drag cards to move them (a group takes its cards with it), the corner to resize. Shift-click adds to the selection; shift-drag on the empty board selects everything in the box; ctrl-a selects all.
    • Hover a card and drag one of the dots on its sides to another card to join them. Select an edge to give it a label, choose its arrows or its colour.
    • Double click (or Enter) opens a heading, edits a text card or renames a group. Delete removes what is selected (and the edges on it); ctrl-z and ctrl-shift-z undo and redo.

    Changes are saved a moment after you stop. If the file changed somewhere else - in another app, in another tab - while you had changes not yet saved, the tab says Changed elsewhere and asks: Load theirs or Keep mine. With nothing unsaved, a change made elsewhere is simply shown.

    From the command line
    orgs canvas                               # every board under the org directories
orgs canvas show plan                     # groups, cards and edges as an outline
orgs canvas add plan 'Write the report'   # a heading: a title, a query, -hash or a picker
orgs canvas add plan pics/map.png         # a file
orgs canvas add plan https://jsoncanvas.org
orgs canvas add plan -text 'An idea'      # a text card (- reads it from stdin)
orgs canvas add plan -group Later -color green
orgs canvas add plan 'Book flights' -in Later    # inside a group
orgs canvas link plan 'Write the report' 'Book flights' -label then
orgs canvas link plan idea jsoncanvas -both      # -both or -none for the arrows
orgs canvas svg plan -out plan.svg        # the board as a picture
orgs canvas new boards/plan               # an empty board

    A card is put in the first free place, reading rows from the top left of the board (or of the group), unless -x and -y say where. link names a card by its id or by words in its title, text, file or url; when the words fit more than one card it says which, with their ids. orgs canvas show plan -json is the board and what each card shows.

    In VS Code
    • Org: New Canvas asks for a name (relative to the server's first org directory, boards/plan) and opens the new board.
    • Org: Add Heading to Canvas puts the heading at the cursor on a board you pick (or a new one). The heading is given an :ID: if it has none, so the card follows it when it is renamed or refiled.

    • A .canvas file opens as JSON by default, so a vault of notes opened in VS Code is not changed under you. Reopen Editor With… → Canvas (orgs / worg) shows worg's board in the tab: drag, connect, edit, and click a heading's card to open it in the editor. The board is saved by the orgs server, never by VS Code. To always open boards this way, add to your settings:

      "workbench.editorAssociations": { "*.canvas": "org.canvasEditor" }

    Both commands and the editor need the canvas feature on (Org: Turn orgs Features On or Off).

    Trackers and heatmap calendars

    With tracker on, a #+TRACKER: line anywhere in a file charts one thing a day: a property you write on your day pages, a tag, a query, a habit, the time clocked under a heading, the words you wrote, or a column of a table. It is a tracker and heatmap calendar in org's own spelling: the options are key:value words, as on a #+PLOT: line, and the data is ordinary properties, logbooks and tables that Emacs reads as it always has.

    * How the year went
#+TRACKER: source:property:MOOD title:"Mood"
#+TRACKER: source:habit:Run color:green goal:1
#+TRACKER: source:clock:Writing type:bar from:-30d
#+TRACKER: source:property:SLEEP type:line from:-60d goal:7:00
#+TRACKER: source:query:"IsDone()" type:bar from:-8w title:"Done"

    The line is never changed; the chart is drawn wherever the file is shown: worg's rendered view and every html export get a heatmap calendar or a line in place of the line, a LaTeX export the same picture in TikZ, a Typst export the picture inline, and the plain text exporter a sparkline with the summary. With the feature off the line is an unknown keyword and exports as nothing, as in Emacs.

    What a tracker follows

    source: names it, as kind:argument (the kind may also be its own key: habit:Run is source:habit:Run):

    source:property:MOOD the MOOD property, a day at a time (below)
    source:tag:gym how many headings tagged :gym: fall on each day
    source:query:"IsDone()" how many headings a query finds on each day
    source:habit:Run the days the habit Run was done (its State "DONE" lines)
    source:clock:Writing minutes clocked a day under Writing and everything below it
    source:clock:* every clock in every file
    source:words words written a day (writing mode's log)
    source:table:weight a #+NAME: weight table: a date column and a value column

    A habit or clock heading is found by its title (the same title, else every title containing the words); clock: also takes a query (source:clock:"HasTags(\"client\")"). A clock that runs past midnight counts on both days. A habit ticked twice in a day is one day.

    The day a value is for

    A property is read from:

    • day pages: a file named for its day - orgs's Wed_2026_11_04.org, org-roam's 2026-11-04.org, org-journal's 20261104 - in its own property drawer at the top of the file, or on a #+PROPERTY: MOOD 4 line. On a week page (dayPageMode: week), a heading called Mon, Tue… is that day of the page's week.
    • any heading with a day: a title that starts with a date (a datetree's 2026-11-04 Wednesday) or a heading under one, then CLOSED, CREATED, SCHEDULED, DEADLINE, then a timestamp in it. date: picks one instead: date:closed, date:created, date:scheduled, date:deadline, date:timestamp, date:title, date:page.
    :PROPERTIES:
:MOOD: 4
:SLEEP: 7:30
:END:
#+TITLE: Wed_2026_11_04

    Tags and queries count headings on the same days, so source:query:"IsDone()" counts each finished task on the day it was closed.

    Values

    A value is read the way it is written:

    4, 72.5kg, 8,000 a number (a unit after it is dropped)
    1:30, 1h30m, 45m, 2h a duration, in minutes
    yes, t, [X] / no, [ ] true or false, 1 or 0
    ★★★☆☆, ⭐⭐, 4/5 a rating

    When a day has several values (two headings that day, a table with two rows), agg: says how they become one: sum (the default for counts, habits, clocks and words), mean (the default for properties and tables), max, min, last or count.

    The options
    type: heatmap (the default: a year of days like GitHub's), line, bar, sparkline
    from: to: the days shown, as orgs sched reads a date: -30d, -1y, 2026-01-01; to: is today
    agg: sum, mean, max, min, last, count
    goal: the value a day must reach to count toward a streak (goal:1, goal:7:00)
    title: the chart's title (the property, habit or query by default)
    color: blue (the default), orange, aqua, yellow, magenta, green, violet, red, or #rrggbb
    min: max: the colour scale's ends (otherwise from the values)
    unit: a word after the values
    file: only files whose path contains this (or whose name matches a glob)
    datecol: col: a table's date and value columns, by number or header (otherwise found)

    Every tracker has a summary: the days with a value, the total and mean, the least and most, and two streaks - the run of days meeting the goal (any value above zero without one) up to today, and the longest. A run up to yesterday is still current: today is not over yet.

    The days as an org table

    A dynamic block takes the same words and writes the days, newest first, with a total, the mean, the days counted and the streak under them; it is refreshed like any dynamic block (orgs dblock).

    #+BEGIN: tracker source:habit:Run from:-14d
#+CAPTION: Run, 2026-10-21 to 2026-11-04, at [2026-11-04 Wed 23:43].
| Date             |           Run |
|------------------+---------------|
| [2026-11-04 Wed] |             1 |
| [2026-11-03 Tue] |             1 |
|------------------+---------------|
| Total            |            11 |
| Mean             |             1 |
| Days             |            11 |
| Streak           | 5 (longest 5) |
#+END:

    empty:t lists the days with nothing too; rows:30 keeps the newest thirty.

    From the command line
    orgs track MOOD                          # a property: a year as a heatmap in the terminal
orgs track source:habit:Run -type sparkline
orgs track clock:Writing -type bar -from -30d
orgs track all                           # every #+TRACKER: line, drawn
orgs track ls                            # where the #+TRACKER: lines are
orgs track log MOOD 4                    # :MOOD: 4 on today's day page
orgs track log SLEEP 7:30 -date yesterday

    The words after orgs track are a #+TRACKER: line's; -type, -from, -to and -color override the line's. -json is the whole series. orgs track log writes the property into today's day page with a line edit: into its own property drawer, or on a week page under the day's heading (made at the end of the page when it is not there). A day page that does not exist yet is made, from dayPageTemplate for today.

    In worg and VS Code

    worg's Trackers tab shows every #+TRACKER: line in the files as a card with its chart, its summary and where it is; hovering a day says its value, and clicking it opens that day's page (or the heading the value came from). A property tracker has a Log today box. New tracker is a builder - what to follow, the chart, how a day adds up, how far back, a goal, a title, a colour - which draws the chart as you go and gives the #+TRACKER: line to copy or add to a file. The pencil on a card opens that card's line in the builder.

    In VS Code a code lens over every #+TRACKER: line shows the last month as a sparkline and the summary, and opens the chart beside the file; a hover says the same. Org: Log Tracker Value writes a property on today's day page (the properties your trackers follow are offered first), Org: Insert Tracker builds a line from a few questions and puts it under the cursor, and Org: Show Trackers opens worg's tab.

    Related notes

    The headings most like the one you are reading, from anywhere in your files, each with a reason: the words the two share most and the sentence of it most like what you are reading. One button links it, and the link is an ordinary org link. Turn it on with orgs features related on.

    Nothing needs setting up: the words engine reads every heading's own text

    • its title (counted twice) and its body up to its first child - and

    compares them by the words they use, rare words weighing more than common ones (BM25, by cosine, so a score runs from 0 to 1). Only prose counts: property and logbook drawers, planning and clock lines, #+ lines, src/example/export/comment blocks, link targets (a link's description counts), urls, timestamps, footnotes and verbatim are left out. Words are lightly stemmed (notes meets note, draining meets drain) and common words (the, which, todo) are not counted.

    A heading asks with its whole subtree; a file with all of its text. What comes back leaves out the heading itself, its parents and everything under it (a file: everything in it), and whatever a link already joins to it - either way, a link from it or one into it. Ask with linked to keep those, marked.

    Embeddings

    With a model, the embeddings engine finds notes alike in meaning even when they share few words. Name a backend in the server's yaml:

    related:
  engine: auto            # auto, words or embeddings
  embeddings:
    backend: ollama       # ollama, local, openai or gemini
    model: nomic-embed-text
    perMinute: 60         # requests a minute, at most
    batch: 16             # headings per request
    blend: 0.25           # how much of the words score is mixed in
    Backend Asks Default model Key
    ollama /api/embed at the assistant's Ollama url (url to change) nomic-embed-text none
    local /v1/embeddings of a local runtime or assistant.local.servers entry (llamacpp:name, lmstudio:name), or url none: name one the server's, if any
    openai /v1/embeddings at api.openai.com (or url) text-embedding-3-small apiKey, else the assistant's chatgpt key
    gemini Google's OpenAI-compatible endpoint gemini-embedding-001 apiKey, else the assistant's gemini key

    Pull the model first (ollama pull nomic-embed-text, or worg's model manager); a llama.cpp server must be started with --embeddings. The server works through your headings in the background, a batch at a time, never more than perMinute requests a minute, and keeps the vectors in <config>_related_vectors.gob beside its yaml, keyed by the heading's text: only a heading whose text changed is asked for again, and a restart asks for nothing. engine: auto answers by embeddings once at least half the headings have one, and by words until then (the answer says which). A heading's question needs no request - it is its subtree's stored vectors - but unsaved text from an editor is embedded when asked.

    Linking one

    Link writes the result under the heading you are reading, at the end of its own text (before its first child), in a Related: list - made the first time, added to after that:

    ** Upgrading the cluster
We drain each node, cordon it, then upgrade the kubelet.

Related:
- [[id:7c0a74bf-404c-4021-9bfd-e4caf7a8917e][Node maintenance]]

    The note linked to is given an :ID: first if it has none, as org-id would. A file with no ID is linked [[file:./other.org][Title]]. The same link is never written twice. A Related: or See also: line you wrote yourself is used as the list.

    From the command line
    Command Does
    orgs related 'Upgrading the cluster' the notes like a heading (a title, query or hash)
    orgs related ops.org [-line 12] like a file, or the heading at a line of it
    orgs related ... -link 2 link the second one
    orgs related ... -engine embeddings choose the engine; -linked keeps linked ones; -n 20
    orgs related text 'some words' like some text (or text on stdin)
    orgs related pairs pairs alike across everything, with no link between
    orgs related status what is indexed, and the embeddings' progress
    orgs related reindex [-embeddings] read everything again (-embeddings: every vector too)

    -json prints the server's answer.

    In worg and VS Code

    worg: the ✨ button in the Files tab's bar opens a Related panel beside the page that follows the heading you are reading (the cursor in the editor or source view, the top of the page in the rendered view), with each result's score, shared words and sentence; click to open it, the link button to link it, the pin to stay on one heading while you look around. The panel also sits in Search's Inspect dialog. The engine (auto, words, embeddings) is chosen in the panel, and the embeddings' progress is at its foot. The Related Notes tab (sidebar and palette) shows how the index stands, reads everything again, and lists Alike, and not linked: the pairs of headings most like each other that nothing links yet, each with a Link button.

    VS Code: a Related Notes view in the Org side bar follows the heading at the cursor, asking about the buffer's own text while it has unsaved changes. Click a result to open it; the inline link button saves the buffer and links it. Org: Show Related Notes opens the view; its title bar pins it, refreshes it and picks the engine.

    Drawings (Excalidraw, org-excalidraw)

    Hand-drawn diagrams kept beside the org files as Excalidraw drawings - the same .excalidraw files excalidraw.com saves, and Excalidraw's markdown form, .excalidraw.md - linked from org the way a picture is. With features: excalidraw: on, worg draws and edits them, every export shows them, and the link stays an ordinary file link that Emacs opens.

    * How a request gets in
The proxy sees it first.

#+CAPTION: The request flow
#+ATTR_HTML: :width 600
[[file:drawings/request.excalidraw]]

    A link with no description is the drawing as a picture, so #+CAPTION:, #+NAME: and #+ATTR_HTML: / #+ATTR_LATEX: work as for any picture. org-excalidraw's [[excalidraw:…]] links are read the same way, and so is a link to an .excalidraw.md. A link with a description stays a link.

    The picture beside it

    Each save from worg writes the drawing's picture next to it: request.excalidraw.svg (Excalidraw's own export, with the scene inside it, so the svg opens again as a drawing in excalidraw.com) and request.excalidraw.png (twice the size, for LaTeX). That is the name org-excalidraw and excalidraw.com's "embed scene" export use, so org-display-inline-images in Emacs shows it when the file links the svg; a markdown Drawing.excalidraw.md gets Drawing.excalidraw.svg.

    A drawing made or changed elsewhere (another app, excalidraw.com, a text editor) has no picture, or one older than the drawing. Then the server draws one itself the first time an export needs it, and keeps it beside the drawing: rectangles, ellipses, diamonds, lines and arrows with their heads, text, freehand strokes, pasted pictures and frames, in plain lines

    • legible, but not Excalidraw's hand-drawn look. The next save from worg

    replaces it with Excalidraw's own.

    Exports

    The html exporter (and so worg's rendered page and the VS Code preview), Typst, reveal.js and the other html exporters show the svg. LaTeX, the pdf and Beamer want a png: the one worg saved while it is as new as the drawing, else one made from the svg by rsvg-convert when that is installed; with neither, the link is left as a link and the server says why on its log. Nothing of this touches the org file: the links are pointed at the picture in the export copy only. A drawing outside every org directory is shown only when a picture is already beside it - the server never writes there.

    What is read
    .excalidraw Excalidraw's json: {"type": "excalidraw", "version": 2, "elements", "appState", "files"}. Pictures pasted into a drawing are kept in it as data urls, as Excalidraw keeps them.
    .excalidraw.md Excalidraw's markdown form: the scene in its compressed-json block (lz-string) or json block, the pictures its ## Embedded Files section names (id: [[cat.png]], found beside the drawing, from the vault root, or by name).

    Saving an .excalidraw.md writes its drawing block back as a plain json block (the plugin reads both and compresses it again on its own next save if it is set to), and makes its ## Text Elements section again from the drawing - the plugin takes text from there over the json, so a stale section would undo the edit. The front matter, the Embedded Files section and anything else written in the file are kept. Pictures pasted in worg into a markdown drawing stay in the json; the plugin keeps its own as vault files.

    In worg

    Drawings in the sidebar (and the palette) lists every drawing under the org directories, newest first, with its picture and the org lines that link to it; the box at the top makes a new one. A click opens it in Excalidraw itself, over the page. It saves with ctrl-s and two seconds after the last change, writing the drawing, its svg and its png; dark mode follows worg's. A drawing changed elsewhere since it was opened is not overwritten: the bar says so and offers Overwrite or Reload theirs.

    In the Files tab, clicking a drawing in the rendered page opens it, and the org editor's New drawing here asks a name and a caption, makes the drawing beside the file, puts the link under the cursor's line and opens the drawing - the unsaved text stays where it was underneath.

    From the command line
    orgs draw ls                                   # every drawing, its picture, what links to it
orgs draw new drawings/flow                    # an empty drawing, from the first org directory
orgs draw new flow -link-from 'Design' -caption 'The flow'   # and its link under a heading
orgs draw svg flow.excalidraw -out flow.svg    # the server's own drawing of it (-saved: the saved one if fresh)
orgs draw open flow.excalidraw                 # worg's editor in the browser

    A drawing is named by its path, its path from the first org directory, or its name when only one drawing has it. -link-from takes a title, a query or a hash, and the picker with -. -json gives the list or the answer.

    In VS Code

    A .excalidraw file opens in worg's drawing editor in the tab (the extension does not carry a second Excalidraw). Hovering over a drawing's link shows its picture, with an Edit drawing link. Org: New Drawing makes one beside the org file, puts its link at the cursor and opens it; Org: Open Drawing opens the one under the cursor, or a list. With the Excalidraw extension (pomdtr.excalidraw-editor) installed, the first open asks which editor to use and remembers it in org.excalidraw.editor (worg saves the pictures exports use; the other extension does not).

    Endpoints

    GET /excalidraw/list, GET /excalidraw?file=, GET /excalidraw/svg?file= (&render=server for the server's drawing), POST /excalidraw/save {File, Scene, Svg, Png, Modified}, POST /excalidraw/new {File, Hash | Filename, Caption}. A save is checked: the scene must be an Excalidraw scene (at most 32 MB), the svg may not run anything (no scripts, event handlers or foreign objects; pictures only as data urls, links only http, https or mailto), the png must be a png, and every file must be inside the org directories. Each is written beside its file and renamed into place.

    Notes on video and audio (org-media-note)

    Notes on a lecture, a talk, a podcast or a voice memo are a list under a heading. Each item starts with a link to its moment in the recording. The links are org-media-note's, so the same file works in Emacs, where they jump mpv to that moment:

    * Week 3 lecture
:PROPERTIES:
:MEDIA: lectures/week3.mp4
:END:
- [[video:lectures/week3.mp4#0:12:30][0:12:30]] the proof starts here
- [[video:lectures/week3.mp4#0:31:05-0:32:10][0:31:05-0:32:10]] worth hearing twice
* A talk
- [[audio:talks/keynote.mp3#0:04:10][0:04:10]] the one slide that matters
* On YouTube
- [[video:https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ#0:00:43][0:00:43]] the chorus
* From the bibliography
- [[videocite:smith2020#0:05:00][0:05:00]] a cited recording
    • video: and audio: name a file (relative to the org file, as Emacs reads it) or a url. YouTube and Vimeo urls play in their own players.
    • videocite: and audiocite: name a citation key. The key's entry in the file's bibliographies (#+bibliography: and citations.bibliography in the yaml) gives its file field first, then its url, which is the order org-media-note uses.
    • #0:12:30 is a moment. #0:12:30-0:12:40 is an A-B loop: the player plays that span over and over. 0:12:30.250 (milliseconds) is read and written too.

    The recording a heading is about comes from the first of these it has:

    1. a :MEDIA: property: a path, a url, a link, or cite:key;
    2. an :AUDIO: property. This is what a voice note writes, so recorded voice notes can be annotated the same way;
    3. a media link in the heading's own text.

    org-media-note keeps no property of its own (it asks mpv what is playing), so :MEDIA: is orgs's. Emacs ignores it and reads the links.

    Turn it on with orgs features mediaNotes on.

    In worg

    The Media Notes panel lists every heading with a recording. The player sits beside its notes:

    • Click a note to jump there. A loop note plays its span until you clear the loop.
    • Type in the note box. The note is stamped with the moment you started typing, and Pause while I type holds the player still meanwhile. ctrl-enter (or Note) writes it among the other notes in time order.
    • A and B mark a loop. With both set, the next note is written as a loop.
    • The panel also has speed control, back and forward five seconds, and Transcribe (see below).
    • Keys, while not typing: k play/pause, j back 5s, l on 5s, n the note box, [ and ] the loop marks, \ clears the loop.

    In a file's rendered view, clicking a timestamp link opens the panel at that moment. alt-click plays it in the page instead.

    In exported pages

    With the feature on, the html exporter draws one player per recording, where its first link is. Every timestamp link on the page then seeks that player, and a loop link loops. The page needs no server for this: a small script comes with it. Links to YouTube and Vimeo get their embedded players. Other exporters, and html with the feature off, keep them as ordinary links.

    From the command line
    orgs media                                   # every heading with a recording
orgs media notes 'Week 3'                    # its notes, by time
orgs media add 'Week 3' 12:30 'the proof'    # a note at a moment
orgs media add 'Week 3' 31:05-32:10 'again'  # an A-B loop
orgs media play 'Week 3' 12:30               # mpv (else vlc, iina, the OS player) from there
orgs media start lectures/week4.mp4 -file school.org -title 'Week 4'
orgs media transcribe 'Week 4' -write        # whisper's words, each a linked note

    The time is the first word that reads as one (12:30, 0:12:30, 12:30-12:45). The words before it name the heading. With no heading named, the one session there is is used, or you pick one. play hands mpv --start and the loop, just as org-media-note does. A file that is not on this machine is streamed from the server.

    In VS Code
    • A media link is clickable. It opens a player beside the text at that moment, looping a loop link. Hovering shows the time and the recording.
    • Org: Open Media Player opens the recording of the heading the cursor is in.
    • Org: Insert Media Timestamp asks the open player for its time (or asks you) and writes the link the way org-media-note's insert does: as a new list item on a blank line or after a note, otherwise at the cursor. The player's Note here button does the same.

    Local files play straight from disk. A citation key is looked up through the server.

    Transcribing

    With a whisper server set up for voice notes (voice: in the yaml), Transcribe in worg, or orgs media transcribe -write, writes whisper's segments under the heading. Each segment becomes a timestamp note, so the transcript can be clicked through like any other notes.

    Callouts (org special blocks)

    Callouts - the coloured boxes with a title and an icon, some of them folding - written the way org already writes a box: a special block. Turn it on with orgs features callouts on. Off, a #+begin_warning block is what it always was (a <div class"warning-block">= in html, an environment in LaTeX); on, every exporter draws it as a callout. Nothing is written into the file either way.

    #+begin_warning Mind the gap
The doors close fast.
#+end_warning

#+begin_tip Take the early train :fold closed
It is half empty.
#+end_tip

#+begin_faq :title "Why: because" :fold open
Because.
#+end_faq

    The block's name is the type; the words after it are the title (or :title "...", for a title with a colon in it); with no title the type's own name is shown. Emacs reads all of this as an ordinary special block, so ox-html writes <div class"warning">= for it and org-special-block-extras users keep their own definitions.

    The types

    The usual callout types, with their aliases and colours (orgs callouts types lists them, and GET /callouts/types is the list every client uses):

    Type Also written Colour Beamer
    note blue block
    abstract summary, tldr cyan block
    info blue block
    todo blue block
    tip hint, important cyan exampleblock
    success check, done green exampleblock
    question help, faq orange block
    warning caution, attention orange alertblock
    failure fail, missing red alertblock
    danger error red alertblock
    bug red alertblock
    example (see below) purple exampleblock
    quote cite grey block

    Three names already mean something in org, so they stay what they are:

    • #+begin_example is org's verbatim block and never a callout. Write an example callout as #+begin_callout Results :type example.
    • #+begin_quote and #+begin_abstract are a callout only when they say so, with a title or a callout argument (#+begin_quote Wilde, #+begin_abstract :fold open). Plain, they are a quote and an abstract.

    #+begin_callout Title :type NAME is the general form, for any type. A type no row names (#+begin_callout :type recipe, or #+begin_recipe Soup :fold open - a block with a callout argument) is drawn as a note, and orgs callouts check warns about it. A special block with no callout argument and an unknown name (#+begin_details) is left alone.

    Folding, icons and colours
    Argument Means
    :fold open folds, starts open (markdown's [!tip]+); also +
    :fold closed starts folded (markdown's [!tip]-); also -, or :fold
    :title "..." the title, in place of the words after the name
    :icon 🍲 an icon of its own: a short text (an emoji), or a type's name
    :color #aa00aa a colour of its own (#hex, a css colour name, rgb(...))

    A folding callout is a <details> in html, so it opens and closes in any browser with no script; printed, it is open. LaTeX, Typst, beamer and plain text show it open.

    What each export makes of it
    • html (and worg's rendered view, and VS Code's preview): a box with the type's icon and title in a bar, a coloured rule down its left and a faint ground of the same colour, in every built-in theme. A dark theme gets lighter titles; the documentation themes (docs, rtd, furo) follow the reader's light or dark setting.
    • LaTeX: a tcolorbox (\begin{orgcallout}{callout-warning}{Mind the gap}), defined in the preamble when the document has a callout.
    • Typst: a #block with the type's fill and a rule down its left.
    • beamer: block, alertblock or exampleblock by type (the table above), the title as the block's title. #+begin_note stays a speaker note in a deck, as it was.
    • reveal.js, deck.js, WebSlides, impress.js: the html box. note and notes stay speaker notes.

    • Plain text (orgs export -f ascii): the paragraphs behind a bar, under a line saying the type and title:

      | WARNING: Mind the gap
|
| The doors close fast.

      (-f txt goes through pandoc, which does not know callouts.)

    • Markdown (orgs export -f markdown): back to markdown's > [!warning]- Mind the gap, so a note can go to a vault and back.

    And the other way: orgs import of a markdown file or a vault of notes turns > [!warning]- Mind the gap into #+begin_warning Mind the gap :fold closed, an [!example] into #+begin_callout :type example, and a type of the vault's own ([!recipe] Soup) into #+begin_callout Soup :type recipe, so each comes back out as it went in.

    From the command line
    orgs callouts                       # every callout in every file, under its heading
orgs callouts ls notes.org          # one file's
orgs callouts types                 # the types, aliases and colours
orgs callouts check notes.org       # warn about unknown types (-check: exit 1)
orgs callouts check -format quickfix   # file:line: lines for vim or Emacs

    orgs lsp (and so any editor using it) warns about an unknown type on the begin line, and offers the callout types when you type #+BEGIN_.

    In worg and VS Code

    worg: in the org editor each callout block is coloured by its type (a rule down the left, a faint ground, the icon on its begin line), folds from its begin line like a heading, and the bar's Callout menu inserts one (type, title and fold) around the selection or on a new line. The rendered view shows them as the html export does, folding ones with their toggles.

    VS Code: the same colouring, an icon and a hover on each begin line, folding, the callout types completed after #+begin_, and Org: Insert Callout (type, title, fold; wraps the selection). The preview is the html export.

    Backlink counts

    With features: backlinkCounts: on, orgs writes beside each heading how many places link to it, counting org links: [[id:…]], [[file:notes.org::*Plans]], [[*Plans]], [[#custom-id]] - every link the backlinks panel already knows. Nothing is written into your files; the counts are worked out from the links that are there.

    orgs features backlinkCounts on
    • A heading's count is the number of places linking to it. A heading with three links to yours counts once (the number of links is in the tooltip). A link from a heading to itself does not count, and neither does a link to the file rather than a heading in it - that one counts for the file.
    • A link's count is how many other links go where it goes, so a link to a heading that six other notes link to as well says ↩ 6.
    • Unlinked mentions - the heading's title or its ROAM_ALIASES / ALIASES written in plain text elsewhere - can be counted too (≈ 2). They cost the server more, so each client has a switch for them, and a title made only of common words ("Notes", "Meeting") is not searched for, as in the links panel.
    In worg

    Each linked-to heading has a small ↩ 3 badge, in the rendered page and in the org editor (where links others share get one too). The editor's badges follow your typing: the server counts the text you have, saved or not. Click a badge and the links panel opens at that heading, with every place linking to it on the line it is written on; click one to go there. The ≈ button in the links panel's header switches mention counts on and off for the badges.

    On the command line
    orgs linkcounts notes.org              # the linked-to headings, ↩ 3 beside each
orgs linkcounts notes.org -all         # the whole outline
orgs linkcounts notes.org -mentions    # ≈ 2 for unlinked mentions too
orgs linkcounts notes.org -links       # every link in the file, and how many others go there
orgs linkcounts -top                   # the most linked headings in the database
orgs links counts notes.org            # the same as orgs linkcounts
orgs linkcounts notes.org -json

    In VS Code

    A code lens over each linked-to heading says 3 backlinks · 2 mentions; clicking it lists the places, each with the line it is written on, and opens the one you pick. Links whose target others link to too get an inlay hint ↩ 4 after them, which lists the places for that target. org.backlinkCounts.style is lens (the default), inlay (↩ 3 ≈ 2 at the end of the headline) or off; org.backlinkCounts.mentions counts mentions. Org: Show What Links Here does it for the heading at the cursor.

    In exports

    Off by default even with the feature on, because a published page is read by people who cannot follow the links. To have html exports write the badge after each linked-to heading:

    server:
  features:
    backlinkCounts: true
  backlinkCounts:
    export: true        # html exports get ↩ 3 after linked-to headings
    mentions: false     # ≈ 2 for unlinked mentions in exports too

    The badge is a <span class"org-backlinks">=, so a theme can style or hide it.

    Places on a map (org-osm)

    With mapView on, every heading that says where it is becomes a pin on a map: the cafe you mean to try, the places a trip went, the people in your contacts. It is a map view in org's own spelling. A place is the :LOCATION: property, the one org itself uses (Emacs's calendar export writes it into an event's LOCATION), so nothing new goes into your files unless you ask for it.

    * TODO Coffee at Revolver                                      :cafe:
:PROPERTIES:
:LOCATION: 49.2834, -123.1090
:END:
* Granville Island market                                      :food:
:PROPERTIES:
:LOCATION: Granville Island, Vancouver
:END:
    What a place can be

    :LOCATION: holds coordinates in any of the ways they are usually written, a link that has them, or words:

    49.2834, -123.1090, 49.2834 -123.1090 decimal degrees, latitude first
    geo:49.2834,-123.1090 a geo: uri (RFC 5870)
    49°17'N 123°7'W, 48.8584 N, 2.2945 E degrees, minutes, seconds, hemispheres
    https://www.openstreetmap.org/?mlat=…&mlon=… an OpenStreetMap link (or #map=z/lat/lon)
    https://www.google.com/maps/place/…/@49.30,-123.14,14z a Google Maps link; a dropped pin wins over the view
    https://maps.apple.com/?ll=…, Bing's cp=lat~lon Apple and Bing links
    [[https://…][Big Ben]] any of those links as an org link
    Granville Island, Vancouver words: an address or a place name

    Also read: :LATITUDE: with :LONGITUDE:, and a contact's :ADDRESS: / :ADDRESS_HOME: / :ADDRESS_WORK: (the records' vcard fields), each its own pin, so somebody with a home and a work address shows twice, labelled.

    Addresses, and looking them up

    Words have to be looked up before they can go on a map. orgs asks Nominatim, OpenStreetMap's own geocoder, by default - one address a second, as its usage policy asks - and keeps every answer in <config>_geocode.json beside the server's yaml, so each address is asked for once. Nothing is looked up until you say:

    orgs map geocode -all                     # every address not looked up yet
orgs map geocode 'Granville Island'       # what the geocoder finds by that name
orgs map geocode 'Market' -write          # this heading's address, kept as :GEO:

    worg's Map tab has a Find them button for the same thing. Set mapView.autoGeocode: true to have new addresses looked up as the map asks for them.

    Coordinates found for an address can be written back beside it, only when you ask (-write, Keep coordinates in worg, Keep as :GEO: in VS Code), so Emacs, a phone or a server with no network has them too:

    :LOCATION: Granville Island, Vancouver
:GEO:      49.270795,-123.134291

    :GEO: belongs to the address beside it: giving the heading another place takes it off (or writes the new one). The name is mapView.geoProperty if you would rather another.

    The Map tab

    worg's Map (in the sidebar while the feature is on) is a real map - OpenStreetMap's tiles, which you can drag and zoom - with every place on it and a list beside it.

    • The query box is the one Search has: IsTask(), HasTags("travel"), IsStatus("NEXT") keep only those headings.
    • Pins are coloured by keyword (none, still to do, done) or by tag (the first tag's colour), with a legend. Pins close together are drawn as one counted circle; click it to zoom in.
    • A pin's card shows the heading's title, keyword, tags and the start of its text, with Open (the heading in Files), Move pin, Edit place… and a link to openstreetmap.org.
    • Place a heading - pick any heading, then click the map where it is or search an address and pick a result. Places not found yet are listed under Not on the map, each with a Place button. A click writes coordinates (to the precision the zoom allows); a picked address is written as you typed it, with its coordinates as :GEO: if you leave Keep the coordinates ticked.
    • Search's row menu has Show on map: the Map tab opens on that heading, or starts placing it if it has no place.
    • The copy button gives a #+MAP: line for what the map shows now (the query, the centre and zoom), to put the map in a page.

    The map follows worg's light and dark modes (dark tiles are the light ones turned, unless mapView.tileDarkUrl names a dark style).

    A map in a page: #+MAP:

    A #+MAP: line draws a map where it stands:

    * Vancouver
#+MAP: title:"Around town" height:340

* Trips
#+MAP: query:"HasTags(\"travel\")" colour:tag title:"Trips"
#+MAP: query:"IsTask()" center:"48.85,2.35" zoom:12

    The words are written as a #+TRACKER: line's:

    query:"…" the headings to show; without one, the places of the heading the line is under and its subtree (the whole file above the first heading)
    center:"lat,lon" where the map is centred (default: fitted to the places)
    zoom:12 0 (the world) to 19 (a street corner)
    height:400 in pixels (default 360); width: likewise (720)
    colour:tag pins by first tag rather than by keyword
    title:"…" a caption
    tiles:nil draw the pins over a grid of degrees, without tiles

    An html export (and so worg's rendered view of the file) shows a picture of the map - OpenStreetMap's tiles composed on the server, numbered pins, each a link to openstreetmap.org - and the places as a numbered list below it. In worg's rendered view the picture becomes the live map. The plain text, LaTeX and Typst exporters write the list (each place linked to openstreetmap.org, with its coordinates). With the feature off the line is an unknown keyword and exports as nothing, as in Emacs.

    Tiles are fetched with a User-Agent naming orgs, two at a time, at most thirty a picture, and kept for a month in the user cache folder (orgs/map-tiles). With mapView.staticTiles: false, or no network, the pins are drawn over a plain grid of degrees instead, so an export never fails for want of tiles.

    From the command line
    orgs map                                   # every place: title, coordinates, file:line, how it was found
orgs map coffee                            # headings whose title has the words (or a query: 'IsTask()')
orgs map -placed -format geojson > places.geojson   # a GeoJSON FeatureCollection for anything else
orgs map set 'Coffee at Revolver' '49.2834,-123.109'
orgs map set Market 'Granville Island, Vancouver' -geo   # look it up now and keep :GEO:
orgs map set Market ''                     # take the location off
orgs map open Paris                        # in the OS's maps (Apple Maps on a mac), or -in osm|google|geo
orgs map status                            # tiles, the geocoder, the cache

    The GeoJSON carries each heading's title, keyword, tags, file, line, hash and an openstreetmap.org link, with marker-color set as the map colours it (github and geojson.io draw it).

    In VS Code
    • Hovering a :LOCATION: line (or :GEO:, :LATITUDE:, an :ADDRESS_…:) shows a small map of the place with its coordinates and links to OpenStreetMap and to worg's Map; an address not looked up yet offers Look it up.
    • Org: Show Map opens worg's Map tab in a panel, on the heading at the cursor when it has a place.
    • Org: Set Location asks where the heading at the cursor is: type an address (the geocoder offers what it finds) or coordinates.
    Settings
    server:
  features:
    mapView: true
  mapView:
    geocodeUrl: https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/search   # any Nominatim-compatible search
    email: ""            # sent with each lookup, as Nominatim asks of heavy users
    autoGeocode: false   # true: look new addresses up as the map asks for them
    geoProperty: GEO
    tileUrl: https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png
    tileDarkUrl: ""      # tiles for dark mode; empty: the light ones, darkened
    attribution: "© OpenStreetMap contributors"
    staticTiles: true    # false: exported maps without tiles

    A tile server of your own (or a commercial one with its key in the url) goes in tileUrl; set attribution to what its terms ask for.

    Timelines

    With timeline on, dated headings become events on a timeline: a history note's people and battles, a project's tasks, a journal's days. It is a timeline in org's own spelling: the dates are org's own timestamps, planning lines and properties, a #+TIMELINE: line says what to draw with key:value words (as on a #+PLOT: or #+TRACKER: line), and Emacs reads the file as it always has.

    #+TITLE: A short history of England
#+TIMELINE: group:tag title:"England, 55 BC to 1603" from:"60 BC" to:1610

* Roman Britain                                                 :era:
:PROPERTIES:
:DATE:     43 -- 410
:END:
* Caesar crosses the Channel                                   :rome:
:PROPERTIES:
:DATE:     55 BC
:END:
* Sutton Hoo ship burial                                      :saxon:
:PROPERTIES:
:DATE:     c. 625
:END:
* Battle of Hastings                                    :war:norman:
:PROPERTIES:
:DATE:     1066-10-14
:END:
* Hundred Years' War                                            :war:
:PROPERTIES:
:DATE:     1337 -- 1453
:END:

    The line is never changed. worg's rendered view puts the live timeline in its place (drag it, zoom it, click an event), an html export the same picture as a still SVG, a Typst export the SVG inline, and LaTeX and plain text exports a chronological list. With the feature off the line is an unknown keyword and exports as nothing, as in Emacs.

    What becomes an event

    Each heading goes on the timeline once, with the first of these it has:

    :DATE: property a free date (below), a point or a span
    an org date range <a>--<b> a span, in its title or its own text
    SCHEDULED: and a later DEADLINE: a span from one to the other
    an active timestamp <2026-11-04 Wed> a point (with a time, at that time)
    CLOSED: a point: when it was done
    SCHEDULED: or DEADLINE: alone a point
    :CREATED: a point
    a datetree day a point: a heading titled 2026-11-04 Wednesday, or under one

    With clocks:t every closed CLOCK: line is a span too (a heading's sittings, under the heading's own lane).

    • Eras: a heading with a span and :TIMELINE: era (or the tag :era:) is drawn as a band across the top with a faint wash down through every lane - a reign, a period, a phase of a project.
    • Leave one out with :TIMELINE: no (or the tag :notimeline:).
    • Colour: :COLOR: (or :TIMELINE_COLOR:) - blue, orange, aqua, yellow, magenta, green, violet, red or a #hex - overrides the lane's colour for that heading.
    History notes: the :DATE: property

    Org timestamps cannot say 44 BC, and are awkward for "about 1200" or "the 1950s". :DATE: takes a date the way a historian writes one:

    1066, 1066-10, 1066-10-14 a year, a month, a day
    1066-10-14 09:30 a moment
    14 October 1066, Oct 14, 1066 the same day in words
    -500, 500 BC, 500 BCE 500 BC (there is no year 0: -1 is 1 BC)
    -44-03-15 15 March 44 BC
    AD 800, 800 CE 800
    c. 1200, ca. 1200, circa 1200, ~1200, 1200? about 1200 (drawn hollow)
    1950s the decade, as a span
    12th century, 5th century BC the century, as a span (1101-1200; 500-401 BC)
    1939-1945, 1939 -- 1945, 1914 to 1918, 500 - 400 BC a span; the end is the end of its year (or month, or day)
    <2026-11-04 Wed>, <a>--<b> an org timestamp or range

    A single day or year is a point at its start; a decade, a century or a range is a span. VS Code's hover on a :DATE: line says how it was read, and orgs timeline date 'c. 1200' does the same in a terminal.

    The #+TIMELINE: line
    query:"HasTags(\"history\")" the headings to draw: a query (any file). Without one, the line draws its own file
    file: only files matching a glob or part of a path; file:all every file
    group: the lanes: tag (a heading's first tag), file, parent (the heading above), keyword, property:NAME, none; auto (the default) picks files when there are several, else parents when they differ, else one lane
    from:, to: the range shown: a free date (-500, 1066, 2026-01-01) or a day as orgs reads one typed (-1y, today, +2w); to:1945 includes all of 1945
    title: the timeline's title
    height: in a rendered page, how tall the view may be before it scrolls (pixels)
    clocks:t clocked time as spans
    limit: the most events (2000; the most recent are kept)

    Lanes take the chart palette's colours in the order they first appear; a lane past the eighth is grey.

    For Emacs readers: #+BEGIN: timeline

    A dynamic block takes the same words and writes the events as an org table - date, a link to the heading, and its lane - which C-c C-c (or orgs dblock) brings up to date:

    #+BEGIN: timeline group:tag from:1300 to:1500
#+CAPTION: Timeline, 7 events, at [2026-11-05 Thu 07:28].
| Date        | Event                                       | Lane   |
|-------------+---------------------------------------------+--------|
| 1337 – 1453 | [[*Hundred Years' War][Hundred Years' War]] | war    |
| 1348 – 1350 | [[*Black Death][Black Death]]               | plague |
| 1381        | [[*Peasants' Revolt][Peasants' Revolt]]     | war    |
#+END:

    A heading with an :ID: is linked by it; one in another file by file:…::*Title.

    In worg

    The Timeline tab (in the sidebar and the palette while the feature is on) shows every dated heading, a #+TIMELINE: line from the files, or a query, in lanes:

    • drag to pan, the wheel or a pinch to zoom about the pointer - from a million years across down to twenty minutes; + - and the arrows from the keyboard, T for today, 0 to fit everything;
    • the axis says what changed at each tick (09:00, then Nov 4 at midnight; Mar, then 2026 in January; centuries as 500 BC, 1, 500), under a band naming the larger unit - the month, the year, the millennium - which stays in view while it lasts;
    • spans are bars with their name inside when it fits, points are dots (hollow when approximate), and names never overlap: a lane grows rows instead;
    • hover an event for its date, how long it lasted, its lane and tags and its first lines; click it to open the heading;
    • a red line marks today; the strip underneath is the whole timeline with the part in view marked - drag it, or click to go there;
    • the lanes picker (tag, file, parent, keyword, a property), "Clocks", and Jump to…, which takes any date :DATE: does (1066, 44 BC, 1950s, today).

    In the Files tab's rendered view a #+TIMELINE: line is the same live timeline, sized to the page; the wheel scrolls the page until you click into it. Open in Timeline ↗ opens the tab on it.

    On the command line
    orgs timeline                          # every dated heading, by year and month
orgs timeline 'HasTags("history")'     # a query's (by century for a long history)
orgs timeline group:tag from:-500      # a #+TIMELINE: line's words
orgs timeline -file project.org -group parent -from -1y -to today -clocks
orgs timeline ls                       # the #+TIMELINE: lines
orgs timeline svg -file history.org -out t.svg   # the exported picture
orgs timeline date '5th century BC'    # how a :DATE: reads
orgs timeline -json | jq '.Events[].Title'

    Spans get a small bar (longer for longer, on a log scale) and how long they lasted; approximate dates a hollow ○, eras ▒.

    In VS Code
    • A code lens over every #+TIMELINE: line (and timeline block): its title, how many events in how many lanes and from when to when; click it to open worg's Timeline on it beside the file.
    • Org: Show Timeline: this file's, a query's, every dated heading, or any #+TIMELINE: line in the files.
    • Hover a :DATE: property to see how it was read (c. 1200 · at 1200 · a year · approximate), or that it was not.
    Endpoints

    GET /timeline/events (line, query, group, from, to, file, here, clocks), GET /timeline/list, GET /timeline/svg (width), GET /timeline/date?text= - see the API section.

    Books, films and games

    Look a book, film, TV show, game or album up in a public catalogue and orgs files it as a heading with its details, its cover and its description, written as an ordinary org record so Emacs reads it the same:

    * Books
  :PROPERTIES:
  :COLLECTION: book
  :END:

** Dune  :fiction:science_fiction:
   :PROPERTIES:
   :RECORD:         book
   :ID:             3ef37370-8e60-4825-8f08-1ed2789b3d5f
   :ADDED:          [2026-11-05 Thu 07:14]
   :AUTHOR:         Frank Herbert
   :PUBLISHED_DATE: 1965
   :PUBLISHER:      Ace Trade
   :PAGES:          544
   :ISBN:           9780441013593
   :URL:            https://openlibrary.org/works/OL893414W
   :MEDIA_ID:       openlibrary:OL893414W
   :IMAGE:          [[file:images/book/dune.jpg]]
   :STATUS:         reading
   :RATING:         4
   :STARTED_DATE:   [2026-11-05 Thu 07:14]
   :END:

   Set on the desert planet Arrakis, Dune is the story of the boy Paul
   Atreides...

    Turn it on with orgs features mediaDb on (or Settings → Org packages in worg, or Org: Turn orgs Features On or Off in VS Code).

    What it looks up, and where
    Kind Catalogues, in the order asked Key
    book Open Library (titles, authors, ISBNs), Google Books none; Google's is optional
    film TMDB, else Wikidata and Wikipedia TMDB needs one
    show (TV) TMDB, else Wikidata and Wikipedia TMDB needs one
    game IGDB, RAWG, else Wikidata and Wikipedia IGDB and RAWG need one
    album MusicBrainz, covers from the Cover Art Archive; Wikidata none
    other Wikipedia none

    So books, albums, and films, shows and games by way of Wikidata work with nothing set up. A catalogue without its key is skipped, and one that cannot be reached is passed over for the next: the search says which were asked and what each answered. Answers are kept for an hour, and MusicBrainz is asked no more than once a second, as it asks.

    An ISBN - typed, pasted with hyphens, or scanned - is looked up directly. Search for an album as OK Computer by Radiohead or Radiohead - OK Computer.

    The heading

    Each one is a record (see Records): :RECORD: book (film, show, game, album, other), so the records browser and collections list them, with fields named so they are shown as what they are - a date, a link, a picture:

    Kind Fields
    book AUTHOR, SUBTITLE, PUBLISHED_DATE, PUBLISHER, PAGES, ISBN, LANGUAGE
    film DIRECTOR, CAST, RELEASE_DATE, RUNTIME
    show CREATOR, CAST, FIRST_AIRED_DATE, NETWORK, SEASONS, EPISODES
    game DEVELOPER, PUBLISHER, RELEASE_DATE, PLATFORMS
    album ARTIST, RELEASE_DATE, LABEL, TRACKS

    and for all of them URL (the page about it at the catalogue), IMAGE (the cover, saved in images/<kind>/ beside the org file and linked relatively), MEDIA_ID (catalogue:id, how orgs knows it again) and STATUS. Genres become tags (science_fiction), the description is the heading's text, and an album's tracks are a numbered list under it.

    The same MEDIA_ID or ISBN already filed is refused, saying where it is, unless you add it again on purpose.

    A new one goes, in this order of preference: where you say (a file and a heading); else where the yaml puts that kind; else under the kind's collection heading; else under a new collection heading (Books, Films, TV shows, Games, Albums) in library.org.

    Shelves and stars

    Every one is on a shelf: up next, in progress, done or set aside - for a book "to read", "reading", "read"; for a film "to watch", "watching", "watched"; "to play", "playing", "played" for a game. The shelf is

    1. the STATUS property, if it has one (any of those words, or want, doing, done, dropped, finished, dnf, on hold…);
    2. else its TODO keyword: a done keyword is done (CANCELLED is set aside), TODO is up next, any other - READING, NEXT, STARTED - is in progress;
    3. else FINISHED_DATE means done and STARTED_DATE in progress;
    4. else up next.

    Moving one to a shelf writes STATUS, and STARTED_DATE when you start it or FINISHED_DATE when you finish it if it has none yet. RATING is 0 to 5 stars, halves allowed (4.5); 8/10 and ★★★★ are read too. A keyword is never changed, so a file kept with TODO=/=DONE stays that way (and STATUS, once written, wins over it).

    A shelf in a document
    #+BEGIN: library :kind book :shelf read :sort rating :limit 10
#+END:

    fills in a table of title (a link to its heading), author, year, status and stars. :kind is any kind or all, :shelf a shelf or one of its words, :sort added (the default), title, creator, year or rating. It is refreshed like any dynamic block (C-c C-c, worg, orgs dblock, and before an export).

    Filling in again

    A heading typed by hand - a title, perhaps an ISBN or an AUTHOR - or one filed before a catalogue knew more can be looked up again: by its MEDIA_ID, else its ISBN, else its title (and author and year to choose among the hits). Only what is missing is written - fields, the cover, the genre tags, and the description when the heading has no text of its own

    • and STATUS and RATING are never touched.
    From the command line
    orgs library search book dune                 the catalogue's hits, with their ids
orgs library add book dune                    choose one in a picker and file it
orgs library add book 9780441013593 -status reading -rating 4
orgs library add film -id movie/329865 -source tmdb -file films.org -under "To watch"
orgs library add album ok computer by radiohead -first
orgs library add other -id Eiffel_Tower -preview   the heading it would write
orgs library ls [book] [-shelf doing]         what you have
orgs library show dune
orgs library set dune -status read -rating 4.5    (or: finish dune, start, drop, rate dune 4)
orgs library refresh "left hand"              fill in what it is missing
orgs library sources                          which catalogues can be asked

    Every command takes -json. Under a pipe, add with several hits refuses and says how to choose (-id or -first) rather than asking.

    In worg and VS Code

    worg's Library tab shows what you have as shelves of covers, by kind, with the stars clickable on every cover; sort by when added, title, author, year or rating, filter by words or a tag. Click a cover for its details: move it to another shelf, rate it, fill its details in again, open its heading. The search box above looks things up; a hit opens with its cover and description, and you choose the shelf, stars and where it goes before adding it. On a phone, the barcode button scans a book's ISBN with the camera (Chrome and Edge on Android, Safari 17+; the page must be on https or localhost).

    VS Code has Org: Add Book, Film or Game… (a live search as you type; put the heading at the cursor as an edit you can undo, have the server write it in this file with the cover saved, or file it where that kind goes), Org: Refresh Media Details and Org: Rate or Shelve Media for the heading at the cursor, and Org: Open Library for worg's tab in a panel.

    Settings
    server:
  features:
    mediaDb: true
  mediaDb:
    contact: you@example.com    # put in the User-Agent, as MusicBrainz and Wikipedia ask
    language: en                # for Wikipedia, Wikidata and TMDB
    noCovers: false             # link the cover's url instead of saving it
    maxTags: 5                  # genres written as tags; noTags: true for none
    keys:
      tmdb: env:TMDB_KEY        # a v3 api key or a v4 read token
      googlebooks: env:GOOGLE_BOOKS_KEY
      rawg: keyring:rawg
      igdbClientId: abc123      # a Twitch application's id and secret
      igdbClientSecret: keyring:igdb
    urls:                       # point a catalogue elsewhere (a mirror, a proxy)
      openlibrary: https://openlibrary.org
    kinds:
      book:
        file: books.org
        under: Reading list     # a heading title or a::b path in that file
        sources: [openlibrary, googlebooks]
        fields: [AUTHOR, PUBLISHED_DATE, ISBN, PAGES]   # only these (MEDIA_ID and STATUS always)
        status: to read         # what a new one starts as
      film:
        capture: Film           # or: a capture template's target

    A key is written as it is, as env:NAME (read from the server's environment) or keyring:NAME (the OS keyring, service orgs). Attribution: book data from Open Library; film and TV data from TMDB ("This product uses the TMDB API but is not endorsed or certified by TMDB"); games from IGDB.com or RAWG; albums from MusicBrainz and the Cover Art Archive; Wikidata (CC0) and Wikipedia text (CC BY-SA). Each heading's URL links back to the page it came from.

    Hover previews

    Rest the pointer on a link and a card shows what it points at: the heading an id: names, a [[*Heading]] of the same file, a heading or a custom id in another file, the start of a whole file, a picture, a pdf, a recording, or a web page's title, description and picture. It works over ordinary org links - nothing is added to your files, and Emacs reads them as it always did.

    orgs features hoverEditor on

    Every kind of link org writes works:

    * Garden
See [[id:6a1e2c4d-…][the soil notes]], [[*Watering]], [[Watering]],
[[file:notes.org::*Soil]], [[file:notes.org::#beds]], [[file:notes.org::42]],
[[file:notes.org]], [[file:plans/bed.png][the bed plan]],
[[file:papers/compost.pdf]] and https://example.com.

    A relative link is read against the file it is written in, as org reads it.

    In worg

    Anywhere worg shows org - the rendered page, the Org view, the editor, search results, kanban card backs, canvas cards - resting on a link for a moment opens its card. Hold ⌘ (ctrl elsewhere) to open it at once.

    • Moving off the link and the card closes it; pin it to keep it.
    • Drag the card by its header to move it (that pins it too), and its corner to size it.
    • A link inside a card opens another card on top of it.
    • Open goes to the heading; Edit turns the card into an editor of the heading's own lines. ⌘S saves them, and only those lines are written. If the file changed since the card read it, the save is refused and says so; Reload reads it again.
    • Esc closes the top card.

    On the command line
    orgs peek id:6a1e2c4d-…                  # the heading, coloured like orgs show
orgs peek '[[*Soil]]' -from notes.org    # read against notes.org
orgs peek file:notes.org::#beds -lines 10
orgs peek https://example.com            # title and description
orgs peek id:6a1e2c4d-… -edit            # open it in $EDITOR at its line
orgs peek id:6a1e2c4d-… -json            # everything the server answered

    In VS Code

    Hovering a link shows its target as text, read straight from the workspace when the file is there and from the server otherwise, with three actions:

    • Open - the target, at its line;
    • Peek - VS Code's peek view on the target, where it can be edited without leaving the file you are in (also Org: Peek Link Target for the link under the cursor);
    • Edit in place - the target's subtree narrowed into a tab of its own; saving it writes it back.
    Settings

    Every key is optional.

    server:
  hoverEditor:
    noWeb: false          # web links show only their address; nothing is fetched
    privateHosts: false   # let a preview fetch addresses on this machine or its network
    timeout: 8s
    userAgent: ""         # default: orgs/<version> (link preview)

    A web page is read by the server, only while the feature is on: its <head> (OpenGraph, then twitter:, then the plain title and description), at most a megabyte, with a timeout, and cached for six hours (ten minutes when it could not be reached). Addresses on the server's own machine and network are refused unless privateHosts is set. The picture is loaded by your browser from the page's site. With no network, a web link's card shows its address.

    Link titles from the web (org-cliplink)

    Paste a web address and get the page's title with it, the way Emacs's org-cliplink does. Nothing new is written into your files: an ordinary org link,

    Watch [[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ][Rick Astley - Never Gonna Give You Up (Official Video)]] later.

    The server reads the page (a browser may not read another site's page, and the command line has no page to read). The title is the page's own, with the site's furniture taken off: " - YouTube", " · GitHub", " - Wikipedia", " - Stack Overflow" and its tag in front, and any " | Site" or " - Site" that is the page's own site name. Videos on YouTube, Vimeo, SoundCloud, Spotify and Flickr are asked through their oEmbed endpoints, which give the video's own title and channel. Brackets in a title become braces, so they cannot end the link early (org-protocol links are written the same way).

    • worg: in the org editor, paste a url on its own. It goes in as [[url][Fetching title…]] at once and the title replaces the placeholder when it comes; the cursor stays where you are. One undo goes back to the plain url, a second takes the paste away. With words selected, the paste makes [[url][those words]] without fetching anything. Shift-paste (ctrl/cmd+shift+v) pastes the url as it is. The capture dialog's body and the heading editor's body do the same. In source blocks, property drawers, #+ lines, tables and inside a link a paste is left alone.
    • Add titles to bare links (the link button in the Files tab's bar and in the editor's bar) lists every bare url and [[url]] in the file with the title its page gives; change any title, untick any to leave it, then Add titles. From the Files tab the server writes the file (and refuses if it changed since the list was made); in the editor the buffer changes, as one undo step, and is saved when you save.
    • VS Code: ctrl/cmd+v in an org file does the same as worg's paste (ctrl/cmd+shift+v pastes plain), and Org: Add Titles to Bare Links lists the buffer's bare links in a pick list.

    • The command line:

      orgs link-title https://orgmode.org/manual/Hyperlinks.html
# [[https://orgmode.org/manual/Hyperlinks.html][Hyperlinks (The Org Manual)]]
orgs link-title -title URL                # the title alone
pbpaste | orgs link-title                 # every url on stdin, one link a line
orgs link-title -filter < notes.org       # the text back with its bare urls titled
orgs link-title -retitle notes.org        # the diff, then asks before writing
orgs link-title -retitle notes.org -dry-run

      -filter is for an editor: in vim, :'<,'>!orgs link-title -filter.

    A url that cannot be read (no network, a page that says 404, a pdf) stays [[url]], and says why. Add titles to bare links leaves alone urls in source, example, export and comment blocks, in property drawers, on keyword and fixed-width lines, in tables (a title would push the columns out of line), inside other links and in verbatim.

    The fetch happens on every paste, so it is careful: http and https only; never a private address (127.0.0.1, 10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, 169.254.x, localhost), checked again on every redirect and on the address actually dialled, unless allowPrivate says otherwise; eight seconds, the first 512kB, one request at a time per site. Titles are kept 30 days (in memory and in the user cache folder, orgs/link-titles.json), so a url pasted twice is asked about once.

    server:
  features:
    autoLinkTitle: true
  autoLinkTitle:
    rules:                       # your cleanups, tried before the built-in ones
      - host: example.com        # also www.example.com, docs.example.com
        strip: [" \\| Example Docs$"]   # regular expressions, removed from the title
    ignore: [docs.google.com]    # never fetched: the paste stays a plain url
    allowPrivate: false          # true: fetch intranet and localhost pages too
    keepSiteName: false          # true: keep " - Site" on every title
    noDefaultRules: false        # true: only your rules
    noOembed: false              # true: never ask a video site's oEmbed endpoint
    cacheFor: 30d
    timeout: 8s

    Quick maths typing (cdlatex)

    Org already reads LaTeX maths in the middle of text: \( … \) and $…$ inline, \[ … \] and $$ … $$ on a line of their own, and an environment such as \begin{equation} … \end{equation} or \begin{align} at the start of a line. Typing it is slow. With latexSuite on, orgs types it the way Emacs's cdlatex does: short triggers expand as you type, TAB moves through the places a snippet leaves to fill, and the maths under the cursor is drawn as you write it.

    * Euler
The identity mk e^{i@p} + 1 = 0
   → The identity \( e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0 \)
dm  sum  n  TAB  TAB  ooo  TAB  1/n^2  TAB  =@p^2/6
   → \[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6} \]

    Nothing in the file is special: what is written is plain org maths, so Emacs, pandoc and every exporter read it as they always have.

    • Into maths: mk makes \( \) and dm a display block (\[ \] on lines of their own); beq and bal make an equation and an align. They work in text, after a space.
    • In maths: @a is \alpha (`a too, as in cdlatex), // a fraction, sr ^{2}, x1 x_1, -> \to, <= \leq, RR \mathbb{R}, sum a sum with its limits, lr( a pair of \left( \right), pmat a matrix, xhat \hat{x}, sin \sin - about 170 of them. Typing a command's name in full (\sqrt) never expands inside it.
    • a/ makes the term before the slash the top of a fraction: (a+b)/ is \frac{a+b}{}, 2\alpha^2/ is \frac{2\alpha^2}{}.
    • In the example above (each step typed with no spaces between) sum wrote \sum_{i=1}^{n} with the i selected: n replaced it, TAB kept the 1, ooo made the top \infty, and TAB went on past it.
    • TAB expands the snippets that wait for it (int, par), jumps to the next place a snippet left (\frac{|}{} then the bottom, then after it), and otherwise moves the cursor out of the bracket it is in. One undo gives back what you typed before a snippet expanded.
    • With a selection, a key wraps it: S in a square root, U under a brace, C crossed out, ( in \left( \right), and in text $ makes it maths.

    orgs keeps the snippets as org tables, so they are yours to change. orgs latex init (or Make my own snippets file in worg) writes latex-snippets.org beside your notes:

    * Mine
| Trigger | Replacement              | Options | Description           |
|---------+--------------------------+---------+-----------------------|
| sr      | ^{2}                     | mA      | squared (as built in) |
| ip      | \langle $1, $2 \rangle$0 | mA      | an inner product      |
| ooo     |                          | mA      | (no ∞ snippet)        |

    Every table in the file with a Trigger and a Replacement column is read. A row with the same trigger and modes as a built-in one replaces it; an empty replacement turns it off. The built-in set is the same kind of file (orgs latex snippets -builtin lists it).
