    • Options: t in text, m in any maths, n inline maths only, M display maths only; A as you type (otherwise on TAB); r the trigger is a pattern, matched against what is just before the cursor, with [[0]] its first group (([A-Za-z])hat → \hat{[[0]]}); w not straight after a letter; v wraps the selection, written ${VISUAL}.
    • Replacement: $1, $2=… are the places TAB visits, =${1:x} one with x already in it, $0 where the cursor ends. The same number twice is typed in both places at once (\begin{$1} … \end{$1}). In a table cell \vert is a | and \n a new line.
    orgs latex snippets                    # every snippet, by group
orgs latex snippets greek              # those with every word
orgs latex expand 'x + @a'             # what typing that becomes: \alpha
orgs latex expand -plain -tab '\( x int'   # the line as it would read
orgs latex check notes.org             # problems in the file's maths
orgs latex check notes.org -format quickfix -check   # for an editor or a hook
orgs latex init                        # latex-snippets.org to edit

    orgs latex expand is for editors with no engine of their own: it reads the mode from the delimiters in what it is given (-mode inline says it outright) and works from the built-in set when no server answers. orgs latex check finds braces that do not balance, a \left with no \right, environments that are not ended (or end another), environments KaTeX and MathJax do not draw, maths that never closes, and $ x$ - with a space after the dollar org reads it as text, not maths.

    In worg's editor the maths the cursor is in is drawn just below it as you type (a small card, light or dark with the page), and the places a snippet left are underlined until TAB reaches them. ⌘⌥L (or Maths snippets in the palette) opens the cheat sheet: every snippet drawn as it comes out, searchable, with the switches - expand as I type, a/ makes a fraction, preview the maths, and draw maths in place, which shows every piece of maths drawn except the one the cursor is in, as org-fragtog does in Emacs. Rendered pages draw the maths with KaTeX.

    In VS Code the same snippets expand as you type in an org file, TAB works in maths, Org: Preview Maths opens a panel beside the editor that draws the maths under the cursor as you type, a hover over maths offers it, and the file's maths is checked when it is opened or saved (the Problems panel). Org: Show Latex Snippets lists them and inserts one, Org: Wrap Selection in a Maths Snippet does the selection ones, Org: Toggle Latex Suite turns the typing off and on.

    An html export draws its maths with KaTeX, loaded from a CDN unless latexSuite.katex names another copy (or off); LaTeX, Beamer and PDF exports pass the maths through as written.

    server:
  features:
    latexSuite: true
  latexSuite:
    snippets: latex-snippets.org   # your own tables, from the first org directory
    noBuiltin: false               # true: only your own snippets
    katex: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/katex@0.16.11/dist   # what an html export loads; "off" for none

    Keep web pictures here (org-download)

    A note clipped from the web links its pictures where they were found, and those links break when the site moves, and show nothing on a plane. This downloads each one beside the notes and points the link at the copy, the way Emacs's org-download writes one. Turn it on with orgs features localImages on.

    Before and after:

    * The lake
  #+CAPTION: The lake at dawn
  #+ATTR_HTML: :width 300
  [[https://photos.example/lake.png]]

  We walked past [[https://photos.example/forest.jpg][the forest]] on the way.
https://cdn.example/photo-1501785888041
    * The lake
  #+DOWNLOADED: https://photos.example/lake.png @ 2026-11-05 10:20:33
  #+CAPTION: The lake at dawn
  #+ATTR_HTML: :width 300
  [[file:images/lake.png]]

  We walked past [[file:images/forest.jpg][the forest]] on the way.
#+DOWNLOADED: https://cdn.example/photo-1501785888041 @ 2026-11-05 10:20:33
[[file:images/photo-1501785888041.jpg]]

    What counts as a web picture. A link to an http or https url whose name ends like a picture (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .avif, .bmp; .svg with svg: true), with or without a description, and a picture's url written on a line of its own. A url with no extension at all (https://cdn.example/photo-1501) is a picture only when its server says so: orgs asks it (a HEAD, or the first kilobyte). Left alone: urls in source, example, export and comment blocks, in drawers and property lines, in headings and in #+ keyword lines, and urls in the middle of a sentence that are not links.

    What is written. Only the lines holding a link change. The description, the #+CAPTION: and every #+ATTR_…: line stay as they were. Above a link that is alone on its line goes org-download's #+DOWNLOADED: url @ time line - above the caption and attributes, never between them and the picture, so the caption still belongs to it. A link inside a paragraph is just pointed at the copy (a keyword line there would end the paragraph). A picture that could not be fetched keeps its web link.

    Where pictures go. images/ beside the org file, so the links are relative and moving the whole folder keeps them (images/{file}/ gives each file its own folder). A picture is named after the url's file name, or a short hash of the url when it has none worth keeping, with the extension its bytes call for. The same picture already in the folder, under any name, is linked rather than downloaded twice.

    Safety. Only http and https. Addresses on this machine or the local network (and cloud metadata addresses) are refused unless allowPrivate: true, checked when connecting, so a name that points at one is refused too. Each picture must really be one (its first bytes are checked, whatever the site claims), at most 20 MB, and one run stops after 200 MB. orgs says who it is in its User-Agent. Hosts in ignore are left on the web.

    Download on save. With auto: true, every save of a file - from Emacs, worg, VS Code or anything else - keeps its new web pictures here, a moment after the save. A site that failed is not asked again for an hour.

    server:
  features:
    localImages: true
  localImages:
    dir: images             # beside the org file; images/{file} for a folder per file
    auto: false             # download on save
    ignore: [example.com]   # hosts (and their subdomains) left alone
    maxImageMB: 20
    maxRunMB: 200
    allowPrivate: false
    svg: false              # svg pictures can carry scripts
    annotate: true          # false: no #+DOWNLOADED: line

    Pictures nothing links any more. After a picture's link is deleted the file stays. orgs images orphans lists the pictures in the pictures folders whose name no org file mentions (nor a canvas, a drawing or other text file in the org directories - a name written anywhere keeps it). -delete asks before deleting them, and only an account that may delete files can.

    From the command line
    orgs images scan trip.org            # the web pictures it links, with sizes
orgs images scan                     # every file
orgs images localize trip.org        # download them and point the links at the copies
orgs images localize -dry-run        # what would be downloaded, every file
orgs images orphans                  # pictures nothing links
orgs images orphans -delete          # ...and delete them (asks; -yes to not)

    Progress goes to stderr, so -json is only the answer.

    In worg

    The file view's bar has a Keep web pictures here button: a list of the file's web pictures with a thumbnail, where each is and how big, a box to leave one out, and a button that keeps the rest here. Settings… under it sets the folder, download on save and the #+DOWNLOADED: line. In the rendered page, a picture still loaded from the web has a faint dashed outline, and hovering it shows On the web · keep here, which keeps that one. In the editor, pasting a picture's url on its own downloads it at once and writes #+DOWNLOADED: and the [[file:…]] link (a paste over selected words, ctrl/cmd+shift+v, and any other url go on to the link title paste as before).

    In VS Code

    Org: Keep Web Pictures Here lists the current file's web pictures to pick from, then has them downloaded (the file is saved first, and read back after). Above each picture still on the web is a Download here lens, and hovering one shows the picture with the same action. Download on save is the server's auto.

    Optional org packages: checklists, edna, noter, remark, expiry, recur, budgets, contents, review, recipes, ledgers

    Turning them on

    The Emacs packages below are ones orgs does the work of. Each is off until you turn it on, and does nothing at all while off: a TRIGGER or EXPIRY property in your files is left alone, and the commands and panels for it say it is off.

    orgs features                 # which are on
orgs features edna on         # turn one on; written into the server's yaml

    worg's settings menu has an Org packages… entry, and VS Code has Org: Turn orgs Features On or Off. All three write the same features: block:

    server:
  features:
    checklistReset: true
    edna: true
    noter: true
    remark: true
    expiry: true
    autoArchive: true
    recur: true
    clockBudget: true
    toc: true
    review: true
    chef: true
    ledger: true

    Only an administrator can turn one on or off, unless the server runs with noAuth.

    Checklists that start again (org-checklist)

    A repeating heading with :RESET_CHECK_BOXES: t has every checkbox in it, and in the headings under it, unticked when it is marked done and comes round again. Its [n/m] cookies follow.

    * TODO Weekly review [3/3]
SCHEDULED: <2026-11-09 Mon +1w>
:PROPERTIES:
:RESET_CHECK_BOXES: t
:END:
- [X] empty the inbox
- [X] read the calendar
- [X] look over the projects

    #+PROPERTY: RESET_CHECK_BOXES t does it for every heading in a file. orgs check -reset (worg: Reset checkboxes on a kanban card; VS Code: Org: Reset Checkboxes) unticks a heading's boxes by hand, whether or not the feature is on.

    Triggers and blockers (org-edna)

    Two properties, in org-edna's language. A BLOCKER stops a heading being marked done; a TRIGGER acts on other headings once it is.

    ** TODO Write the draft
:PROPERTIES:
:BLOCKER: previous-sibling
:TRIGGER: next-sibling todo!(NEXT) scheduled!("++1d")
:END:

    Finders gather headings, and the action or condition after them works on what they gathered:

    Finders self parent children first-child last-child descendants ancestors siblings siblings-wrap rest-of-siblings next-sibling next-sibling-wrap previous-sibling ids(a b) match("+work") olp("file.org" "A/B")
    Options children(todo-only), todo-and-done-only, no-comment, no-archive
    Actions todo!(NEXT) scheduled!("+1d") deadline!("fri") tag!("a:b") set-property!("P" "v") delete-property!("P") set-priority!("A") set-effort!("1:00") archive! chain!("P")
    Conditions done? todo-state?(WAITING) headings? has-property?("P" "v") has-tags?("a") matches?("+x") re-search?("regexp"), each negated with !
    Other consider(any) / all / a count / a fraction, and if ... then ... else ... endif in a TRIGGER

    A BLOCKER with finders and no condition waits for them all to be done (edna's !done?). Dates in scheduled! and deadline!: +2d from the date the target has (or today), ++2d from now, -1w, cp (copy this heading's), rm, or anything orgs sched takes (mon, tomorrow 10:00). A todo! that finishes a heading runs that heading's own TRIGGER too, five deep at most and never the same heading twice.

    The blocker is checked wherever a heading is marked done (the CLI, worg, VS Code, MCP), and IsBlocked() in a query counts it. -force goes past it.

    orgs edna                      # a heading's TRIGGER and BLOCKER, and what done would do
orgs edna -check 'ids(a1) !done?' -blocker
orgs edna -names               # every finder, action and condition

    orgs lsp marks a TRIGGER or BLOCKER it cannot read, and completes the names as you type.

    Notes on a PDF (org-noter)

    A heading with :NOTER_DOCUMENT: is a session, and the headings under it with :NOTER_PAGE: are its notes, in page order - org-noter's own shape, so a session started in Emacs opens in worg and the other way round.

    * Attention is all you need
:PROPERTIES:
:NOTER_DOCUMENT: papers/attention.pdf
:NOTER_PAGE: 4
:END:
** Scaled dot product
:PROPERTIES:
:NOTER_PAGE: (4 . 0.31)
:END:
#+begin_quote
We suspect that for large values of d the dot products grow large
#+end_quote
Hence the √d.

    worg's Noter panel shows the document beside its notes: select a passage to note it, click a note to go to its page. VS Code's Org: Open PDF Notes opens the same panel.

    orgs noter                                   # every session
orgs noter notes                             # a session's notes, page by page
orgs noter add -page 4 -y 0.3 -quote '...' 'the note'
orgs noter start reading.org papers/x.pdf

    Highlights and margin notes (org-remark)

    Highlight a passage of any file and keep a note on it without touching the file: the highlights live in a marginalia file, org-remark's, so Emacs reads them too.

    remark:
  notesFile: marginalia.org   # relative to the first org directory

    In VS Code, Org: Highlight Selection works in any editor and the highlights are drawn there; worg highlights in a file's Org view. When the file changes, a highlight is found again by its words.

    orgs remark                                  # every file with highlights
orgs remark show notes.txt                   # file:line:col, for a quickfix list
orgs remark add notes.txt 'the words' -line 7 -note 'why'
orgs remark note ID 'a better note'
orgs remark rm ID

    Headings that expire, and old done work (org-expiry, auto archive)

    With expiry on, a heading whose :EXPIRY: has passed is filed away. The value is a date, or a span after its :CREATED::

    * An article to read
:PROPERTIES:
:CREATED: [2026-11-04 Wed 10:00]
:EXPIRY: +2w
:END:

    With autoArchive on, a heading in a done keyword that was closed longer ago than after is archived. :AUTO_ARCHIVE: nil on a heading (or a heading above it, or the file's #+PROPERTY:) keeps it; :AUTO_ARCHIVE: 7d archives it sooner.

    expiry:
  handler: archive   # archive, sibling, tag (adds :ARCHIVE:) or keyword
  keyword: EXPIRED
  every: 1h
autoArchive:
  after: 30d
  mode: archive      # archive, sibling or tag

    The server looks every every. To see and do it yourself:

    orgs expire               # what is due, and why
orgs expire -run          # file it away
orgs expire -set +2w      # give a heading an EXPIRY (a span or a date)

    worg's Expiry & Archive panel lists what is due with a button to file it away, and a search row's menu has Expires…; VS Code has Org: File Away Expired and Old Done Items and Org: Set Expiry.

    Repeats in plain words (org-recur)

    A recurrence written in the heading's title, between bars. When the heading is marked done it is not closed: its SCHEDULED moves to the rule's next date after today and its keyword goes back to the first open one, as a repeat does - a State line in the logbook, :LAST_REPEAT:, no CLOSED.

    * TODO Water plants |+2|
SCHEDULED: <2026-11-04 Wed>
* TODO Pay rent |1,15|
* TODO Standup |wkdy 09:30|
* TODO Gym |Mon,Thu|

    Between the bars is a comma separated list; the rule's next date is the earliest of them. These are org-recur's spellings (org-read-date's):

    +2 +2d +w +2w +1m +1y that long from today (+w is a week)
    +0 . today
    Mon thursday Sun,Sat the next such weekday
    1 15 1,15 the next such day of a month (31 skips the short months)
    wkdy the next weekday, Monday to Friday unless recur.weekdays says
    +tue +2tue -fri the next (second) Tuesday after today; the Friday before
    12-25 dec 25 25 Dec 12/25 the next such day of the year
    2027-01-01 that date
    10:00 3pm Mon 09:00 Thu 10:00-11:00 a time, alone (today if still to come, else tomorrow) or with any of the above

    A weekday, day of the month or day of the year that is today counts as the next one, not today: |Thu| finished on a Thursday goes to next Thursday. (org-read-date would say today.) A rule with no time of day keeps the time the stamp had.

    Which date moves: SCHEDULED; else DEADLINE when that is the only date the heading has; else a SCHEDULED is added. A stamp that also carries an org repeater (SCHEDULED: <2026-11-02 Mon +1w>) moves by the rule, once - the cookie is kept as written but not stepped as well. Any other repeating date on the heading moves on by org's own rule.

    Bars that are not a rule (* a | b | c) are left alone: the heading is simply done. IsRecurring() finds the headings that have one.

    orgs recur                          # every heading with a rule: in words, and its next dates
orgs recur set 'Water' '|Mon,Fri|'  # give a heading a rule (a query or hash, then the rule)
orgs recur clear 'Water'            # take it off
orgs recur explain '|1,15|' -n 6    # what a rule means, and its next dates
orgs search 'IsRecurring()'

    worg draws the rule as a chip after the title - ↻ every 2 days · Fri 6 Nov - in the search rows and the agenda, and a search row's menu has Repeats…, which shows the next dates as you type.

    In VS Code the rule gets the same note after it and a hover with its next dates, a | in a heading offers common rules, and Org: Set Recurrence sets or clears the rule of the heading at the cursor.

    server:
  features:
    recur: true
  recur:
    weekdays: "mon,tue,wed,thu,fri"   # what |wkdy| stands for

    Not done: org-recur's org-recur-finish-done and -archive (they are about finishing a heading without a rule, which here is just marking it done), its own org-recur-schedule-today (orgs sched today does that), and the rest of org-read-date's spellings (ISO weeks such as 2026-W45, words such as tomorrow).

    Time budgets (org-clock-budget)

    With clockBudget on, a heading can be given a time allowance for a period, and the time clocked under it in that period - the heading's own clocks and every heading below it - is set against the allowance. The property names the period:

    * Writing the book
:PROPERTIES:
:BUDGET_WEEK: 5:00
:BUDGET_MONTH: 20:00
:END:
** TODO Chapter one

    BUDGET_DAY, BUDGET_WEEK (Monday to Sunday), BUDGET_MONTH, BUDGET_QUARTER (from January) and BUDGET_YEAR. A value is H:MM or a plain number of minutes (org-clock-budget's two spellings), or 5h, 90m, 1h30m. A budget is the heading's own, not inherited, and comes round again each period: nothing carries over. A clock that is running counts up to now, whether Emacs is running it (an open CLOCK: line) or orgs is.

    Each budget also has a pace: how far through the period it is now. On a Wednesday at noon a week is 36% through, so 1:48 of a 5:00 budget is on track and 4:00 is spending ahead of the week.

    Clocking in under a heading that is already over budget says so in the answer ("Writing the book is over its budget: 5:30 of 5:00 this week"), and a clock that runs past a budget raises a notification once. Settings:

    clockBudget:
  dailyHours: 12   # hours a day that can be budgeted (org-clock-budget's default)
  notify: true     # false: no notification when a running clock goes over

    dailyHours makes the budgetable time of a period (12 hours × 7 days is 84 hours a week), which the report compares the budgets given out against.

    From the command line:

    orgs budget                          # every budget, with bars against the pace
orgs budget -period week -over       # this week's, only those over
orgs budget -date 2026-10-15         # the periods around another day
orgs budget clocked                  # what the running clock is spending
orgs budget set 'Writing' week 5:00  # give one (off takes it away)

    In a file, org-clock-budget's report as a table, refreshed like any dynamic block:

    #+BEGIN: clockbudget :period week,month :scope agenda
#+END:

    :period is one or more periods (default: every one somebody has a budget for), :scope agenda (every file, the default) or file, :date another day. The last two rows are org-clock-budget's sums: budgeted against clocked, and budgetable hours against what is given out.

    Queries: HasBudget() / HasBudget("week") and OverBudget() / OverBudget("month").

    worg's Time Budgets tab shows each period's budgets as bars with a mark for the pace, steps back and forward a period at a time, opens a heading on a click, and sets, changes or takes off a budget (Add a budget finds a heading by its title). While the clock runs under a budgeted heading, the header shows a chip beside the focus timer: used against budget, red once over. VS Code shows the same in the status bar, and has Org: Show Clock Budgets and Org: Set Clock Budget (for the heading at the cursor).

    Tables of contents (toc-org, org-make-toc)

    A list of links to a file's headings that keeps itself current: every time the file is saved - from Emacs, worg, VS Code or anything else - orgs brings it up to date. Turn it on with orgs features toc on. Three ways to ask for one, and a file may have all three.

    toc-org's way: a heading tagged :TOC:. Its whole body is the list; any text you write there is replaced (planning lines and drawers directly under the headline stay). Only the first :TOC: heading in a file is written.

    * Table of Contents :TOC:
- [[#about][About]]
  - [[#installation][Installation]]
- [[#use][Use]]

* About
** Installation
* Use
    Tag Means
    :TOC: two levels deep, github-style links ([[#about][About]])
    :TOC_3: three levels deep
    :TOC_2_gh: github-style links, said outright
    :TOC_2_org: org links ([[*About][About]]), which Emacs follows with no help
    :QUOTE: beside it the list inside a #+BEGIN_QUOTE block

    @ may stand for _ (:TOC@2@org:), as in toc-org. Levels are counted from the top of the file. Left out: the :TOC: heading itself, headings tagged :noexport: or marked COMMENT (with everything under them), and under a :noexport_1: heading its children (:noexport_2: keeps one level of them, and so on). A heading with a CUSTOM_ID is linked by it. Keyword, priority, tags and [1/3] cookies are not part of an entry (a cookie would change the list every time a box is ticked), and a link in a title shows as its description. Two headings with one title are #notes and #notes-1.

    org-make-toc's way: a :TOC: property and a :CONTENTS: drawer. The list goes in the drawer and the text around it stays. A :TOC: property with no drawer under it is a setting for the tables above it, not a table.

    * Contents
:PROPERTIES:
:TOC: :include all :ignore this
:END:
Some words before the list.
:CONTENTS:
- [[#about][About]]
:END:
    Setting Means
    :include all the whole file (the default)
    :include descendants the headings under this one
    :include siblings this heading's siblings and what is under them
    :depth N on the table's heading: N levels from where it starts. On any other
    heading: N levels of what is under it, in every table that lists it
    :ignore this leave this heading out (what is under it is still listed)
    :ignore descendants leave out what is under it
    :ignore siblings leave out its siblings
    :local depth this heading's :depth is only for its own table, not tables above it
    :force depth / :force ignore this table ignores the :depth / :ignore of the headings it lists
    :links org org links instead of github ones (ours; org-make-toc chooses in elisp)

    A list goes in parentheses: :ignore (this descendants). The old values all, children, siblings on their own still read.

    A dynamic block. Anywhere, refreshed on save like the others and by orgs dblock:

    #+BEGIN: toc :depth 2
- [[*About][About]]
  - [[*Installation][Installation]]
#+END:

    :depth, :include as above (of the heading the block is under), and :links gh. Org links are the default here. The heading the block is under is not listed.

    The links work everywhere orgs shows a file: the exported page and worg's rendered view go to the heading, whichever kind the table uses.

    orgs toc                          # bring every file's tables up to date
orgs toc notes.org                # one file
orgs toc -check                   # write nothing; exit 1 if any table is stale
orgs -local toc -check            # the same with no server (a git hook, CI)
orgs toc -print notes.org         # what the tables should say
orgs toc -insert notes.org        # add a * Table of Contents :TOC: heading
orgs toc -insert notes.org -make-toc -line 12   # org-make-toc's drawer at line 12's heading

    worg: the table of contents button in the Files tab's bar (Update, Insert a :TOC: heading, Insert a Contents heading), and the same button in the org editor, which works on the text being edited; saving from the editor brings the tables up to date first.

    VS Code: Org: Update Table of Contents, Org: Insert Table of Contents (a :TOC: heading, a :CONTENTS: drawer at the heading at the cursor, or a #+BEGIN: toc block), and the tables are brought up to date on save (org.toc.updateOnSave, on by default). Both work on unsaved text.

    Headings that come back to be read (org-review)

    With review on, a heading can be given a cadence: it comes back to be read again every so often. This is for areas, projects and notes you want to look at regularly (a monthly look at your finances, a quarterly look at each project), not for tasks with a date. orgs reads and writes org-review's own properties, so the same files work in Emacs:

    * Areas
:PROPERTIES:
:REVIEW_DELAY: +2w
:END:
** Health
:PROPERTIES:
:LAST_REVIEW: [2026-10-01 Thu]
:END:
** Money
:PROPERTIES:
:REVIEW_DELAY: +1m
:LAST_REVIEW: [2026-10-20 Tue]
:NEXT_REVIEW: [2026-11-20 Fri]
:END:
    • :NEXT_REVIEW: is when it is next due. When it is set, it wins.
    • Otherwise the heading is due on its :LAST_REVIEW: plus its delay.
    • :REVIEW_DELAY: is the delay (+3d, +2w, +1m, +1y). It is inherited from the headings above and from the file's #+PROPERTY: REVIEW_DELAY. With none of those, orgReview.delay is used (+1m). Above, Health is due two weeks after 1 October.
    • A heading with a REVIEW_DELAY of its own and no dates has never been reviewed, so it is due now. In the example that is Areas.
    • A heading takes part only when it has one of the three properties itself. With orgReview.unreviewed: true, a heading that only inherits a delay is due too. This is org-review's org-review-unreviewed, and it flags every heading under that delay.
    • Archived, commented and finished headings are never due.

    Marking a heading reviewed writes LAST_REVIEW as today, and NEXT_REVIEW as today plus the delay. Changing the cadence moves NEXT_REVIEW to the last review (or today) plus the new delay. Snoozing moves only NEXT_REVIEW.

    orgReview:
  delay: +1m          # the cadence of a heading with no REVIEW_DELAY
  setsNext: always    # always, only-future or never (org-review-sets-next-date)
  stamp: inactive     # [2026-11-04 Wed]; active writes <2026-11-04 Wed>
  unreviewed: false

    (review: is a different block. It configures the weekly review wizard, which is not this.)

    orgs reviews                         # what is due, most overdue first
orgs reviews -within 7               # and what falls due this week
orgs reviews walk                    # one at a time: r reviewed, s snooze, c cadence, u undo, o open
orgs reviews done 2 -note 'on track' # the second one; a note goes into its log drawer
orgs reviews done 'Money'            # by title, a query or a hash
orgs reviews set Money +1w           # its cadence; -next fri, or -clear to stop reviewing it
orgs reviews snooze Money +3d
orgs search 'ReviewDue()'            # the query functions ReviewDue() and HasReview()
orgs agenda -view R                  # today's agenda, then what is due for review

    worg has a Due for Review panel. It shows the due headings one at a time, with their text rendered, and takes one key per decision: r reviewed, R reviewed with a note, s snooze, c change the cadence, o open, → next, u undo. A search row's menu has Review every…. In the weekly review, the stale items step also lists what is due for review.

    VS Code has these commands:

    • Org: Mark Heading Reviewed
    • Org: Set Review Cadence
    • Org: Headings Due for Review: a list that opens the heading, with buttons that mark it reviewed or snooze it.

    VS Code also puts a line over each heading in review (for example "20 days late · every 2 weeks"). Click it to mark the heading reviewed.

    Recipes from web pages (org-chef)

    Give orgs the address of a recipe page and it writes the recipe as a heading, the way org-chef does in Emacs, so one cookbook file serves both:

    * Weeknight Chicken Curry
:PROPERTIES:
:source-url: https://spiceandsimmer.example/chicken-curry/
:servings:   4
:prep-time:  15 min
:cook-time:  25 min
:ready-in:   40 min
:IMAGE:      [[file:images/recipes/weeknight-chicken-curry.jpg]]
:RECORD:     recipe
:END:
A creamy, mild curry that's on the table in 40 minutes.

** Ingredients
- 2 tablespoons vegetable oil
- 1 large onion, finely chopped
- 1 1/2 pounds boneless chicken thighs

** Directions
1. Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat.
2. Add the onion and cook until soft, about 8 minutes.

    The page is read for its schema.org recipe data, which nearly every recipe site carries (WordPress recipe plugins, the big recipe sites, the newspapers). A page with steps in sections ("For the sauce") gets a heading per section under Directions. orgs adds two properties org-chef does not write and does not mind: :IMAGE:, the picture, saved beside the org file in images/recipes/, and :RECORD: recipe, which lists the recipes in the records browser too.

    A heading is a recipe when it has :source-url: (org-chef's, written by either), :RECORD: recipe, or both an Ingredients and a Directions child - so a recipe typed by hand from org-chef's manual capture template counts. Times may be written as org-chef writes them (15 m) or as orgs does.

    orgs chef add https://www.example.com/recipes/curry          # into recipes.org
orgs chef add https://… -file cook.org -under Mains           # under a heading
orgs chef add https://… -dry-run                              # show the heading, write nothing
orgs chef ls chicken                                          # recipes with chicken in them
orgs chef show curry -servings 6                              # scaled for six
orgs chef cook curry                                          # one step at a time
orgs chef shop curry burgers -servings 4                      # a shopping list

    • Scaling multiplies each ingredient's leading amount and keeps its spelling and units: 1/2 cup doubles to 1 cup, ½ cup to 1 cup, 1 1/2 pounds halves to 3/4 pound, 2-3 teaspoons doubles to 4-6, 400g to 800g. Only the leading amount changes, so 1 (16 ounce) can doubles to 2 (16 ounce) cans. Large amounts are rounded as a cook would (150 g, not 150 1/3 g). A recipe that does not say what it serves scales by a factor instead (-factor 2). Nothing is written: the file keeps the recipe as it was.
    • A shopping list adds the same thing in the same unit up across recipes (2 cups rice and 1 cup rice are 3 cups rice) and is written as a heading of checkboxes with a [0/n] cookie: under a Shopping heading in the recipes file when there is one, else at the end of the first recipe's file, or where -file and -under say.
    • A page already in a file (the same :source-url:) is not added again unless asked (-force, or Add anyway).
    • Some sites turn servers away; worg and the api take the page's html pasted in (Html on /chef/fetch and /chef/add).

    worg's Recipes tab takes a pasted address, shows what was read before anything is written and lets you pick the file and heading; it lists the recipes with their pictures and searches them by name and ingredient. A recipe opens with a servings stepper, ingredients to tick off (kept in the browser, not the file), Cook - large type, one step at a time, the arrow keys to move, and the screen kept awake where the browser can - and Add to list for the shopping list.

    VS Code has Org: Import Recipe from URL (put in the open file at the cursor, as an edit you can undo, or written by the server with its picture), Org: Scale Recipe (the recipe at the cursor, scaled, to copy or insert) and Org: Make a Shopping List from Recipes.

    server:
  features:
    chef: true
  chef:
    file: recipes.org      # where a recipe goes when no file is named (made if missing)
    checkboxes: false      # ingredients as - [ ] items (org-chef writes plain - items)
    noRecord: false        # leave out :RECORD: recipe
    noPictures: false      # keep the picture's url instead of saving it

    Ledger journals (ledger-mode, ob-ledger)

    Money kept the way ledger and hledger keep it - plain-text transactions - in source blocks of an org file, or in .ledger, .journal, .hledger and .dat files under the org directories. With features: ledger: on, orgs reads them itself: balances, registers, monthly totals and checks work without ledger or hledger installed.

    * Accounts
#+NAME: opening
#+BEGIN_SRC ledger
commodity $
  format $1,000.00

2026/01/01 * Opening
    Assets:Bank:Checking     $3,000.00
    Equity:Opening
#+END_SRC

* This year
#+BEGIN_SRC ledger :cmdline reg Expenses
2026/02/07 ! (1042) Grocer  ; :food:
    Expenses:Food:Groceries    $98.10
    Expenses:Food:Snacks       $12.00
    Assets:Bank:Checking     = $2,889.90
#+END_SRC
    One journal or one block

    All the ledger and hledger blocks of a file are read in order as one journal: the second block's assertions are checked against the first block's balances, and its accounts and commodities are the first's. This is what every report, the dynamic block and the checks read.

    ob-ledger runs each block alone, and so does running a block (C-c C-c, orgs code at, worg's Run). Any report can be asked for one block alone too: -block 1 (its place, from 0), -block opening (its #+NAME:) or block=line:12.

    What is read
    Dates 2026/11/04, 2026-11-04, 2026.11.04, 11/04 with Y 2026 (or year); 2026/11/04=2026/11/05 for the auxiliary date
    The first line status * or !, a code (1042), the payee, ; a note (hledger's payee \vert note too)
    Postings an account, then two spaces (or a tab) and the amount; (Budget:Rent) virtual and unbalanced, [Savings] virtual and balanced; one posting may leave its amount out
    Amounts $1,000.50, -$5, $-5, 10 AAPL, 1.000,00 EUR, "M&M" 3; decimal-mark , for commas
    Costs 10 AAPL @ $150, @@ $1500, {$150} lot prices; two commodities and no cost read as an exchange
    Assertions Assets:Bank $-50 = $950 checked; Assets:Bank = $950 with no amount is an assignment; =, * as hledger has them
    Metadata ; :tag1:tag2: and ; Key: value on a transaction or a posting
    Directives account, commodity (and its format), include (only inside the org directories), alias a=b and alias /re/=b, apply account, D, P prices, Y=/=year, comment … end comment
    Skipped, with a warning periodic ~ and automated = transactions, value expressions, directives it does not know

    An unbalanced transaction, a failed assertion, a date that is not a day and an amount that does not read are errors, each at the line it is on - the org file's own line for a block.

    Reports
    orgs ledger                                  # balance of every journal, as ledger bal prints it
orgs ledger bal -source money.org -depth 2
orgs ledger bal Expenses not Rent -period 'this year'
orgs ledger reg ^Assets:Bank -period 'last month'
orgs ledger monthly Expenses -depth 2        # a month a line, an account a column
orgs ledger check                            # file:line problems; exits 1 on an error
orgs ledger check -format quickfix
orgs ledger sources
orgs ledger -f money.ledger bal              # a file here, no server at all

    Words after the report are account regular expressions, any of which may match, as ledger's are; not leaves the next ones out. Periods are said in words: this month, last year, 2026, 2026-11, nov, q3, from 2026-01-01 to 2026-04-01, jan..mar, since last month - the end is not included. -json gives the rows.

    A dynamic block writes a report into the file as an org table, refreshed with orgs dblock (or C-c C-c in Emacs with orgs' blocks):

    #+BEGIN: ledger :report balance :account Expenses :period "this year" :depth 2
| Account  | Balance   |
|----------+-----------|
| Expenses | $2,755.50 |
| \_  Food | $355.50   |
| \_  Rent | $2,400.00 |
|----------+-----------|
| *Total*  | $2,755.50 |
#+END:

    :report is balance, register, monthly or check; :source is another journal (the file the block is in when it has ledger blocks, every journal otherwise); :block, :account, :period, :begin, :end, :depth and :real as above.

    Running a block

    Running a ledger block runs ledger -f as before, and an hledger block now runs hledger -f (it used to run ledger). When the program is not installed and the feature is on, orgs answers the block itself for a :cmdline of bal, reg or accounts with -p, -b, -e, --depth, --real, --flat and account patterns; anything else says to install ledger. A journal with an error answers with the error, as ledger does.

    In worg and VS Code

    worg's Ledger tab: a journal (or one block of it) and a period at the top; the account tree with balances, opened and folded by its arrows; pick an account to see its month-by-month totals as bars (a table one click away) and its register with a running total, each row opening its line. The journal's problems are listed above, each a link to its line.

    VS Code marks unbalanced transactions and failed assertions in ledger blocks as you type, shows an account's balance when you hover on it, and has Org: Ledger Balance and Org: Ledger Register, which print the report in the Org Ledger output.

    Org files in any editor: orgs lsp

    What it is

    orgs lsp is a language server: any editor that speaks the Language Server Protocol - Neovim, Helix, Zed, Sublime Text, Emacs (eglot), the JetBrains IDEs, VS Code - gets these for org files from it:

    • Completion: TODO keywords after the stars (the file's #+TODO:, else the server's), tags after a heading's colon (this file's first, then every tag the server knows), link targets after [[ - headings, #custom-id=s, =<<targets>>, file: with every org file, file:x.org::* with that file's headings, and id: with every heading that has an ID, found by its title - #+ keywords and blocks, source block languages and property names.
    • Go to definition on a link: [[*Heading]], [[#id]], [[target]], [[file:x.org::*Heading]], [[file:x.org::42]] and [[id:...]], which the server finds in whichever file has it.
    • Clickable links for urls, files and the linkProtocols in your yaml.
    • The outline (document symbols): headings with their keyword, tags and date, and named blocks and tables under the heading they are in; and every heading of every file as a workspace symbol.
    • Folding of headings, blocks and drawers.
    • Diagnostics: a block with no #+END_, a drawer with no :END:, a link to a heading, file or id that is not there, and the Harper or LanguageTool lints of orgs lint, whose suggestions are quick fixes.
    • Code actions: schedule, deadline, refile (recent targets first), archive, and run the source block, #+CALL: or inline code under the cursor - with a ▶ Run lens over every block the server would run.

    In VS Code (Org Everywhere starts it for you): broken links, an unclosed drawer and an unclosed block in the Problems panel, and a hover on one.

    The outline, folding and the links within a file work with no server. The rest is one request each to orgs serve, as for every other command.

    Setting an editor up

    The server is orgs lsp on standard input and output. Its flags: -lint auto|harper|languagetool|all|off (default auto, the first checker the server offers), -lang, -dialect, -ignore RULES, -refile-depth N and -path-map SERVER=LOCAL for a server on another machine. The same can be sent as initialization options: lint, lang, dialect, ignore, refileDepth, pathMap (an object).

    Neovim
    vim.lsp.config('orgs', { cmd = { 'orgs', 'lsp' }, filetypes = { 'org' }, root_markers = { '.git' } })
vim.lsp.enable('orgs')
    Helix (languages.toml)
    [language-server.orgs]
command = "orgs"
args = ["lsp"]

[[language]]
name = "org"
scope = "source.org"
file-types = ["org"]
language-servers = ["orgs"]
    Emacs (eglot)
    (add-to-list 'eglot-server-programs '(org-mode . ("orgs" "lsp")))
    Zed, Sublime Text, JetBrains

    Any "custom language server" setting that takes a command: orgs lsp, for files ending .org.

    How edits are made

    An editor holds text the server has not seen yet. So schedule, deadline and run send the buffer to the server, which makes the edit it would make to the file and sends back the text; the difference arrives as one edit you can undo, and the file on disk is not touched. Nothing needs saving first.

    Refile and archive change two files, so they work on the files: they refuse while the buffer has unsaved changes ("save first"), and afterwards bring the buffer up to what the server wrote if the editor did not reload it by itself.

    The commands behind the actions can be bound to keys with workspace/executeCommand, which is also how to schedule for a date the menu does not offer:

    Command Arguments Notes
    orgs.date uri, line, name, value? SCHEDULED=/=DEADLINE; value as orgs sched reads it
    orgs.run uri, line needs babel.enable
    orgs.refile uri, line, {Filename, Olp}? asks where when the target is left out
    orgs.archive uri, line 
    -- Neovim: schedule the heading under the cursor for Friday
vim.lsp.buf.execute_command({ command = 'orgs.date',
  arguments = { vim.uri_from_bufnr(0), vim.fn.line('.') - 1, 'SCHEDULED', 'fri' } })

    Babel: Python Sessions

    :session keeps one python running for a file, so that a block can use what an earlier block made - the way the cells of a notebook share a kernel:

    #+PROPERTY: header-args:python :session analysis :results output

#+BEGIN_SRC python
import statistics
xs = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
#+END_SRC

#+BEGIN_SRC python
statistics.mean(xs)
#+END_SRC

#+RESULTS:
: 2.8

    Only python has sessions; a :session on any other language is ignored and each block runs on its own, as before. :session none, or no :session at all, is a fresh python for every block.

    • A session belongs to its name and its org file. Two files with :session main have one each.
    • Like a notebook, the value of a block's last line is shown after what it printed (:results output), or is the whole result (:results value). A line ending in ; is not shown.
    • A matplotlib figure the block drew is saved where :file says (further figures get -2, -3…), or under <file>_files/ when it says nowhere, and linked in the result.
    • A pandas table that is the block's value comes back as an org table.
    • An exception is written as the result, the traceback in place of the output, as a notebook shows it. The run still reports that it failed.
    • !ls, %pip install, %matplotlib inline, %%bash and their commonest relatives work, so a cell pasted from Jupyter runs.
    • A block that runs past babel.timeout is interrupted (a KeyboardInterrupt, which keeps the session); one that ignores that is killed, and the session starts again next time.
    • A session left alone for an hour stops, and every session stops with the server. POST /babel/sessions/stop stops one now, which is how a notebook is run again from the top.
    • :python /path/to/venv/bin/python picks the interpreter, as in org; babel.commands.python does it for every file.

    Babel: Results, Calls And Inline Code

    What org's C-c C-c does, from any client: run what is at a line and write what it produced into the file.

    Results

    A block's result is written under it as #+RESULTS:, replacing the one that was there. Its shape follows :results:

    Written Comes out as
    (text, short) : line for each line
    (text, ten lines on) an #+begin_example block
    table an org table
    list an org list
    file [[file:...]]
    raw the text as it is, to be read as org
    drawer inside a :RESULTS: drawer
    html, latex an export block
    code, org a source block
    silent, none nothing written
    append, prepend added to what is there instead of replacing it
    pp python's value pretty printed (:results value pp)
    link, graphics with :file: the code writes the file itself, and the result is the link

    :results words come in groups - collection (output, value), type (table, list, scalar, verbatim, file…), format (raw, drawer, pp, link…) and handling (replace, append, silent…) - and, as in org, a word nearer the block replaces an inherited one of its own group: :results replace on a block undoes a file's header-args :results append.

    A block named with #+NAME: writes #+RESULTS: name, so another block can take it as a variable. :eval no (or never) is never run. :eval query runs only when somebody runs it - that block, at its line, or something they ran that needs it - and never on a schedule, in a run of a whole file or from a tangle, because there is nobody to ask. Exporting never runs a block, so never-export, no-export and query-export run like yes.

    Where header arguments come from

    As in org, four layers, each merged over the one before, key by key:

    1. babel: defaultHeaderArgs: in the server's yaml, for every block (org's org-babel-default-header-args);
    2. babel: languageHeaderArgs:, for one language (org-babel-default-header-args:python);
    3. the header-args property, then header-args:<lang>;
    4. the block's #+HEADER: lines, then its own line.
    babel:
  enable: true
  defaultHeaderArgs: ":exports both"
  languageHeaderArgs:
    python: ":session main :results output"

    A property is set by #+PROPERTY: header-args ... lines (a #+SETUPFILE:'s among them, where it stands) or a heading's :header-args: in its property drawer, and the nearest setting wins outright: a heading's :header-args: :results silent replaces the file's whole value, so a :session the file gave is gone under it. Written header-args+ (on a heading or a #+PROPERTY: line) it adds to what is above instead. header-args and header-args:python are separate properties, each inherited on its own. Tangling reads them the same way.

    Exports read them too: a block whose own lines say nothing about :exports is exported as what it inherits (code, results, both, none). When nothing says, the code is shown with its results; org's own default is code, which defaultHeaderArgs: ":exports code" gives.

    A block that fails (a non-zero exit) has what it printed and what it wrote to standard error written as its result, so the error is in the file where the answer would be. :stderr yes adds standard error after the output of a block that worked (for programs that warn, or answer there).

    Around the program and the result

    Header Does
    :prologue "text" put before the program (after its variables)
    :epilogue "text" put after it
    :wrap the result in #+begin_results … #+end_results
    :wrap example … in any block: :wrap src python, :wrap quote
    :post fmt(x=*this*) run block fmt with *this* standing for the result, and write what it returns instead
    :cache yes run only when the code or its inputs changed: the result is written as #+RESULTS[hash]: and a run with the same hash leaves it be
    :stdin name a table (or result) by name as standard input - for awk, which reads its program from a file

    Noweb

    With :noweb yes (or eval, no-export, strip-export, strip-tangle), a block's <<name>> is replaced by the code of block name (or of every block whose :noweb-ref is name) before it runs, and <<name(args)>> by the result of running name with those arguments, as a #+CALL: would. Text before a reference on its line is repeated on every line it brings in (:noweb-prefix no turns that off). Tangling reads references the same way.

    Calling a block

    #+NAME: double
#+BEGIN_SRC python :var n=1
return n * 2
#+END_SRC

#+CALL: double(n=21)

    runs double with n set to 21 and writes the result under the call. A call names its block by #+NAME:, looked for in its own file first and then in every file the server watches, so a file of useful blocks works as org's library of babel. Header arguments may go in square brackets after the name or after the arguments: #+CALL: double[:results raw](n=2) :results table.

    Inline code

    src_python{return 6*7} and call_double(n=4) in a paragraph run in place, and their result follows them as {{{results(=42)}}}=. An inline result has to fit on a line.

    Variables

    :var x=name takes a table by its name, the result of a named block (which is run first), a #+RESULTS: name already in a file, a named list (its items) or a named example block (its text). other.org:name names one in another file, relative to this one.

    An index picks part of a table or list, counting from 0 as org does, rules included: data[2,1] a cell, data[,0] a column, data[1:3] rows 1 to 3, data[-1] the last row, * everything at that level.

    A table's first row is its column names when a rule is under it: they are taken off before the block sees the table and put back on its result when that is a table the same width (:colnames no passes the header as data, :colnames yes always takes the first row, :colnames '(a b) names the result's columns). :rownames yes does the same with the first column. Rules are left out unless :hlines yes, which passes them as the language's null (None, nil…).

    Every language gets its variables in its own way: an assignment before the code for python, ruby, perl, lua, R, javascript, powershell and shell (a table as tab separated text); package-level var=s for go (a body with no =package main and func main is wrapped in them, as ob-go does, and :imports "os" "strings" adds imports); a let round the program for emacs-lisp; -v name=value for awk; and $name substituted in the SQL for sqlite (a table as the path of a csv file with its header, for .import; :db names the database, :colnames yes or :header prints a header, and the answer comes back as a table). A table handed to gnuplot is written to a file and bound as its name, so plot data using 1:2 works as it does in org.

    Files

    Header Does
    :file name.png the result is this file: a picture drawn there, or what the block printed written into it
    :file-ext png with no :file, a block named plot writes plot.png
    :output-dir dir where a relative :file goes (relative to :dir)
    :file-desc text the link's description, [[file:plot.png][text]]; with no text, the file's name
    :file-mode (identity #o755) the file's mode once it is written (#o644, 0600 too)
    :mkdirp yes make the file's directory when it is missing

    Compiled and other languages

    Language Runs Notes
    C, C++ cc, c++ -std=c++17, then the program :includes, :defines "N 10", :flags, :libs "-lm", :main no; a body without main() is put in one; a table is a const char* 2D array with name_rows, name_cols
    rust rustc, then the program a body without fn main() is put in one
    java java Main.java (JDK 11+) :classname, :imports; a body without a class is put in main
    julia, haskell (runghc), clojure, scheme (guile), octave the interpreter variables in each one's syntax
    sql psql, mysql or sqlite3 =:engine postgresql\ mysql\ sqlite=, :dbhost, :dbport, :dbuser, :dbpassword (mysql), :database; $name in the query is a variable; the answer is a table
    latex pdflatex, then pdftocairo :file eq.png, .svg or .pdf; a fragment is set in the standalone class

    A block that does not compile has the compiler's complaint as its result. babel.commands still replaces what runs (c: ["clang"]).

    Pictures

    dot (graphviz), plantuml, ditaa, mermaid (mmdc) and gnuplot blocks draw a picture where :file says, and the result is a link to it. The picture's format follows the file's extension.

    Ledgers

    A beancount block is a journal, asked a question by bean-query: the question is :cmdline (BALANCES when it says none), and the answer comes back as an org table. A ledger block runs ledger -f over itself with :cmdline as the report (bal by default), and an hledger block hledger -f. With features: ledger: on and the program not installed, orgs answers a bal, reg or accounts :cmdline itself (with -p, -b, -e, --depth, --real, --flat and account patterns), the block read alone as ob-ledger reads it.

    #+BEGIN_SRC beancount :cmdline "SELECT account, sum(position) GROUP BY account"
2026-01-01 open Assets:Bank
...
#+END_SRC

    :cmdline works for every language: its words go after the code's file on the command line, split on spaces with quotes holding words together, and never through a shell.

    Bable Block Execution

    TODO: Fill in information on babel and literate programming

    Capture

    The capture tool can take a quick snippet of text and turn it into a targetted org entry in a file of your choosing. With Refile capability Capture can be a major asset when helping you organize your thoughts.

    Configuration for the system is done through the captureTemplates entry in your orgs.yaml file:

      captureTemplates:
    - name: "BasicEntry"
      type: "entry"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "BasicItem"
      type: "item"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "BasicCheckItem"
      type: "checkitem"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "BasicPlain"
      type: "plain"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "BasicTable"
      type: "table-line"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "Datetree"
      type: "entry"
      target:
        type: "file+datetree"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "OlpDatetree"
      type: "entry"
      target:
        type: "file+olp+datetree"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures::Level1::Level2"

    The template string

    A template may also carry a template: of its own, which is the shape of what gets captured. The server does nothing with it - it hands the client's headline and content to the file exactly as they arrive - so the string is a form for the client to put up: worg reads it in worg/src/capture.ts and turns it into boxes to fill in, and anything else talking to /capture is free to do the same or to ignore it.

       - name: "QuickNote"
     type: "entry"
     target:
       type: "file+headline"
       filename: "notes.org"
       id: "Inbox"
     template: |-
       :PROPERTIES:
       :CREATED: {{now}}
       :SOURCE:  {{source|Where did this come from?}}
       :END:
       {{CONTENT}}

    Note the |-. A yaml scalar written over several lines without it folds its newlines into spaces, so the whole template arrives as one line - which is a property drawer that is not a property drawer. Use a block scalar for anything longer than one line.

    The syntax is four spellings of one thing:

    Written Means
    {{CONTENT}} The body - one big box, and where a
    dictation or a pasted picture lands
    {{name}} A value to fill in, labelled from the
    name
    {{name\vert prompt}} The same, asked for in your own words
    {{name\vert =value}} Pre-filled with a default, still editable
    {{name\vert prompt\vert =value}} Both

    The last two are written by the server, not by whoever writes the template.

    Some names answer themselves, and the server answers them. A placeholder whose name is in the table below is answered on the way out of /capture/templates, and the answer is written in as that placeholder's default:

      :CUSTOM_ID: {{uuid}}         ->  :CUSTOM_ID: {{uuid|=f81d4fae-7dec-...}}
  :CREATED:   {{now}}          ->  :CREATED:   {{now|=[2026-09-29 Tue 14:05]}}
  :WHEN: {{now|When was it}}   ->  :WHEN: {{now|When was it|=[2026-09-29 ...]}}

    A default rather than a substitution, because both halves matter:

    • a client that knows nothing about any of this has a usable value in the box already, so :CUSTOM_ID: {{uuid}} works without a line of client code - and crypto.randomUUID is secure-context only in a browser, so for worg served over plain http from another machine the server is the only end that can answer it at all;
    • a client that would rather answer it itself still sees the name, and can ignore the default - which a substitution would have taken away. A value written in as literal text is a value nobody can change, and the timestamp on a capture is very often the one thing somebody does change: a thing captured today did not necessarily happen today.
    Name Becomes
    {{uuid}} / {{guid}} f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6
    {{shortuid}} js3xiyiy - 8 characters, a-z and 2-7
    {{daypage}} worklog/Mon_2026_09_28.org - the
    current day page, relative to the
    first org directory
    {{username}} / {{user}} ian - whoever asked
    {{hostname}} the machine holding the org files
    {{date}} 2026-09-29
    {{time}} 14:05
    {{datetime}} 2026-09-29 14:05
    {{today}} / {{active}} <2026-09-29 Tue>
    {{now}} / {{inactive}} [2026-09-29 Tue 14:05]
    {{timestamp}} [2026-09-29 Tue 14:05]
    {{tomorrow}} <2026-09-30 Wed>
    {{yesterday}} <2026-09-28 Mon>
    {{week}} 2026-W40
    {{month}} 2026-09
    {{year}} 2026
    {{day}} 29
    {{weekday}} Tuesday
    {{dayname}} Tue
    {{epoch}} / {{unix}} 1790690700
    {{iso}} / {{rfc3339}} 2026-09-29T14:05:00Z

    So a capture that wants an id of its own needs nothing but the property:

       - name: "Note"
     type: "entry"
     target:
       type: "file+headline"
       filename: "notes.org"
       id: "Inbox"
     template: |-
       :PROPERTIES:
       :CUSTOM_ID: {{uuid}}
       :CREATED:   {{now}}
       :AUTHOR:    {{username}}
       :SOURCE:    {{source|Where did this come from?}}
       :END:
       {{CONTENT}}

    Four things about the answering (internal/common/captemplate.go is the grammar, internal/app/orgs/capturefill.go the wiring):

    1. A name with no answer is left standing, braces and all, so a client's reading of a template is unchanged by this pass: it sees fewer holes, never different ones.
    2. One value per name per template, aliases counted as one name, so {{uuid}} written twice in one template is the same uuid both times and a :CUSTOM_ID: and an id: link to it in the body agree. Two templates in one answer get two uuids, because they are two different captures.
    3. It is idempotent. A placeholder that already carries a default is left alone, so a template cannot collect a second answer however many times it goes past.
    4. They are answered when the list is asked for, not when the capture is made. worg re-asks every time its capture dialog opens and orgs cap asks once per run, so a uuid is fresh per capture; a client that holds one list open all day and captures from it twice would offer the same uuid twice.

    /ext/capture/templates, which is where a user edits their own templates, is deliberately not answered: it hands back the template as written, or saving one back would bake this afternoon into it for ever.

    A line whose only content was a placeholder nobody filled in is dropped rather than written empty, so a template offering three optional properties writes the one that was answered.

    A template with no string at all asks for a headline and a body, which is what every example above is.

    Placeholders in the target filename

    The same names work in target: filename:, answered when the capture is made. There is nobody to ask at that point, so a name that does not answer itself (and has no |= default) refuses the capture rather than make a file called {{project}}.org.

       - name: "DayLink"
     type: "entry"
     target:
       type: "file+headline"
       filename: "{{daypage}}"
       id: "Inbox"
   - name: "Scratch"
     type: "entry"
     target:
       type: "file+headline"
       filename: "tmp/{{date}}_{{time}}_{{shortuid}}.org"
       id: "Notes"

    In a filename every value is made filename safe: brackets dropped, spaces to _, colons to -. So {{now}} is 2026-09-29_Tue_14-05 and {{time}} is 14-05. {{daypage}} keeps its /, being a path. A missing folder is created.

    A filename that comes out as the current day page, when that page does not exist yet, is created the way orgs daypage creates it - from the day page template, with last week's open tasks - rather than as an empty file.

    The filename is answered separately from the template body, so a {{uuid}} in both is two different uuids.

    Clock Table

    Time clocked under headings, summed. Two ways to get one:

    • orgs clocktable -block thisweek (and GET /clockreport) report every file at once, straight to the terminal;
    • a #+BEGIN: clocktable dynamic block writes the report into the file and rewrites it whenever it is refreshed. See Dynamic Blocks for its parameters.

    A range is one of:

    Written Means
    today, yesterday, today-N a day
    thisweek, lastweek, thisweek-N a week, Monday to Sunday
    thismonth, lastmonth, thismonth-N a month
    thisyear, lastyear, thisyear-N a year
    untilnow everything ever clocked
    2026-10-04, 2026-10, 2026 that day, month or year
    2026-W40, 2026-Q3 that ISO week, that quarter

    A clock running across the edge of the range counts only the part inside it, and one still running counts up to now.

    Clocking

    TODO: Fill in information on how to use the orgs clocking features

    Constants

    Constants are names a table formula can use. They are not template values; for those see Template values.

    • #+CONSTANTS: vat=0.2 shop=Corner anywhere in the file makes $vat and $shop available to every table in it.
    • The properties of the heading a table sits under are there as $PROP_NAME: :RATE: 40 is $PROP_RATE.
    • pi, t, f, True and False are always defined.

    Constants are text, not numbers: wrap one in value() to calculate with it, as in $2=$1*(1+value($vat)). The table formula guide (Tables) has the full story.

    Day Page

    The day page module is designed to quickly create a worklog file for you every day. It is driven off a template file:

    daypage.tpl

    This template file will expand into a new worklog file when asked. I tend to operate with a single day page per week as I find a daypage per day is to verbose and a daypage per month is to messy.

       dayPagePath: "C:/path/worklog/"

    My personal day page template looks about like so at the moment.

       #+TITLE:  {{day_page_title}}
   #+AUTHOR: Me Myself

   * Inbox

   * Mon
   * Tue
   * Wed
   * Thu
   * Fri

    Detangling and Auto-Tangling

    Detangle

    Tangling writes code out of an org file; detangling brings edits made to the tangled file back into the org blocks they came from (org's org-babel-detangle). It needs the markers a tangle writes with :comments link (or both):

    # [[file:setup.org::*Install][Install:1]]
brew install ripgrep
# Install:1 ends here

    orgs detangle install.sh reads the file, finds each marked section, and writes its code back into that block with a line edit - the block's own indentation kept, org's comma escape put back where a line would read as a heading. -dry-run says what would change. A block whose code has noweb <<references>> is left alone: the tangled file holds their expansion, and that cannot be put back as one block's code.

    Put :comments link on every block with #+PROPERTY: header-args :comments link.

    Auto-tangle

    A file that says so is tangled every time it is saved:

    #+auto_tangle: t

    Only files that ask: nothing is tangled on its own otherwise. A tangled file that says the same as before is not rewritten. One that has been edited by hand since orgs last wrote it is not overwritten: the tangle stops for that file and says so (an event, and the server log), so detangle it, or tangle it by hand with orgs tangle -w to throw the edit away.

    Dynamic Blocks

    A dynamic block is a part of a file that orgs writes for you and rewrites on request: a clock report, a column view, a list of headings a query finds. Everything between the #+BEGIN: and #+END: lines is replaced; nothing else in the file is touched.

    #+BEGIN: clocktable :scope file :maxlevel 2 :block thisweek
#+END:

    Refresh one with orgs dblock FILE LINE, every block in a file with orgs dblock FILE, and every block anywhere with orgs dblock -all (a cron line that keeps the week's clock tables current).

    clocktable

    The time clocked under headings, the way org writes it: one time column per outline level, a bold total, and a file column when more than one file is reported.

    Parameter Meaning
    :scope file (default), subtree, tree / treeN, agenda (every file), or a list
    of files: ("work.org" "home.org")
    :maxlevel deepest level listed (default 3)
    :block today, yesterday, thisweek, lastweek, thismonth, lastmonth,
    thisyear, lastyear, today-3, thisweek-2, untilnow, 2026-10-04,
    2026-10, 2026-W40, 2026-Q3, 2026
    :tstart start of the range, as a timestamp or a typed date (<2026-10-01>, -2w)
    :tend end of the range, exclusive
    :match an org tags match (+work-meeting); only matching headings count their time
    :query an orgs query (IsStatus("DONE")); only matching headings count their time
    :indent nil to write titles without the \_ indentation
    :fileskip0 with several files, leave out the ones with no time

    Weeks start on Monday, as they do in org. A clock that crosses the edge of the range counts only the part inside it, and a clock still running counts up to now.

    columnview

    org's column view written as a table.

    Parameter Meaning
    :id local (the heading the block is under, default), global (the whole
    file), file:notes.org, or a heading's ID / CUSTOM_ID
    :format a #+COLUMNS: line; otherwise the file's own, then the server default
    :maxlevel deepest level listed
    :hlines t for a rule between every row, N for one above each level <= N
    :indent t to indent the ITEM column by level
    :skip-empty-rows t to leave out rows with nothing but a title
    :exclude-tags (tag1 tag2) - headings carrying any of these are left out

    Summed columns (%EFFORT{:}) show the rollup. A #+TBLFM: line under the table is kept and run again after every refresh.

    query

    The headings an orgs query finds, as a table.

    #+BEGIN: query :q "IsStatus(\"NEXT\")" :columns "TODO ITEM FILE DEADLINE" :link t
#+END:

    :q is required. :columns defaults to TODO ITEM FILE and takes the names a #+COLUMNS: line takes, with or without their %. :scope file keeps to this file, :limit N stops after N rows, :link t makes each title a link to its heading.

    insertdatetime

    The moment the block was refreshed, as an inactive timestamp. :active t writes an active one, :format "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M" writes it your way.

    toc

    A table of contents of the file, as a list of links (needs orgs features toc on, which also refreshes it whenever the file is saved). :depth N stops N levels down, :include all (default), descendants or siblings of the heading the block is under, :links gh writes [[#anchor][Title]] links instead of [[*Title][Title]]. The heading the block is under, :noexport: and COMMENT headings are left out.

    Any other name is looked up among the dynamic blocks plugins register.

    Exporters

    TODO: Fill in information on working with exporters

    Finding Source Blocks

    GET /code answers with every #+BEGIN_SRC block the server holds, read rather than merely located: its language, the name another block would call it by, its switches, its babel header arguments, and its variables.

    The variables are the reason this endpoint exists rather than a grep. A variable may be a literal, or it may be the name of something else in the file - a table, a list, the results of another block - and there is no way to tell which by looking at the text. The database knows, so each variable comes back with what it resolves to and where that thing lives:

    #+NAME: monthly
| month | sales |
|-------+-------|
| Jan   |   120 |
| Feb   |   180 |

#+NAME: chart
#+BEGIN_SRC python :var data=monthly :var scale=2 :results file
  ...
#+END_SRC

    data comes back as a reference to a table of two columns and three rows; scale comes back as a literal. A name that resolves to nothing comes back with an empty kind, which is worth saying out loud: it is a block that cannot run.

    Parameter Meaning
    lang Only blocks in this language
    q Only blocks matching this text

    q is matched against the code, the name, the language, the heading, the file and the variable names - somebody looking for a block remembers any one of those.

    Importing A Jupyter Notebook

    orgs import analysis.ipynb (or worg's new file dialog, "Import a Jupyter notebook") turns a notebook into an org file that runs: every code cell a #+BEGIN_SRC block, its outputs the #+RESULTS: under it, and the whole file one python session, so running the blocks top to bottom is running the notebook.

    #+TITLE: Penguin measurements
#+PROPERTY: header-args:python :session penguins :results output
#+STARTUP: inlineimages

* Loading the data
#+BEGIN_SRC python
df = pd.read_csv("penguins.csv")
df.shape
#+END_SRC

#+RESULTS:
: (344, 7)
    • The title is the notebook's own (metadata.title), else its first heading, else its file name.
    • Markdown becomes org: headings (so code lands under the heading it sat under), emphasis, inline code, links, pictures, lists, quotes, fenced code, tables and rules. $…$ and $$…$$ are left alone, since org reads them as they are. HTML that has no org spelling goes in an export block.
    • Outputs are written the way running the block writes them, so running it again replaces them rather than adding to them: printed text as =: = lines, a simple html table (a pandas dataframe) as an org table, a picture saved beside the file in <name>_files/ and linked, a traceback with its colours taken out. A cell with several outputs has them in a :results: drawer.
    • A cell that drew a picture says :file where, so running it again draws over the same picture.
    • Pictures pasted into markdown cells (attachment:) are saved too.
    • Raw cells become export blocks.

    nbformat 4 is read, and 3 as far as its cells go; anything older is refused with a message saying so.

    Keeping Blocks Current

    Some of a file is worth recomputing on its own: a source block that reports disk use or a CI status table, a clock table, a column view, a table's formulas. orgs reruns them on a timer, writes what changed with line edits (nothing else in the file moves), and hands an export a freshly computed copy so a published page is never stale.

    Scheduled source blocks

    A source block, or a #+CALL: line, with a :schedule header argument is run again on that schedule and its #+RESULTS: updated. It needs babel.enable, as running any block does.

    #+NAME: disk
#+BEGIN_SRC sh :schedule 1h :results table
df -h / /home | awk '{print $1, $5, $6}'
#+END_SRC

#+CALL: ci-status(repo="orgs") :schedule 15m

    The schedule is a length of time (30m, 1h, 2d, 1w, 1h30m), a word (hourly, daily, weekly), or a time of day (daily 07:30, 07:30: once a day, at or after that time). The shortest is a minute. Like any header argument it can be inherited: #+PROPERTY: header-args :schedule 1h puts every block in the file on the hour.

    A run that produces what the file already says writes nothing, so a block checked every five minutes does not rewrite its file every five minutes.

    Refreshing dynamic blocks and tables

    • :refresh 1h on a dynamic block's #+BEGIN: line refreshes that block.
    • #+REFRESH: 1h in a file refreshes all of its dynamic blocks and runs every #+TBLFM: in it.
    • refresh.every in the server settings does that for every file that has a dynamic block or a table formula.

    A table is written only when its values change, never just to realign it.

    On export

    An export (/file/html, orgs export, orgs site, typst and beamer pdfs) reads a copy of the file with its dynamic blocks refreshed and its table formulas run, in memory: the page is current and the file is not written because somebody exported it. refresh.onExport: false turns this off, and refresh=f on a request skips it once.

    Settings

    server:
  refresh:
    every: 1h          # every file's dynamic blocks and table formulas
    onExport: true     # default
    scheduled: true    # run :schedule blocks (default; babel.enable must be on too)
    tick: 30           # seconds between looks at what is due

    orgs refresh lists everything on a timer, when it last ran and how it went; orgs refresh run runs it now.

    Refile

    TODO: Fill in information on orgs server refiling

    Running A Source Block

    POST /code/run runs one #+BEGIN_SRC block and hands back what it produced, read the way org reads a babel result rather than as a lump of text: a table comes back as an org table, a list as an org list, a :results file as a link.

    It is off unless it is turned on, under babel: in the server settings. Reading somebody's org files and executing the programs inside them are different promises, and the second is made deliberately.

    What gets run

    The block's code, with its variables written in front of it in the language's own syntax. A :var scale=2 becomes an assignment; a :var data=monthly naming a table becomes that table as a list of lists, so the code can walk it. This is the whole point of babel and the reason the variables were resolved in the first place.

    Two languages take their code and not their variables: go and emacs-lisp are compiled or scoped in ways that do not survive a prepended assignment, and a variable silently missing is worse than one that was never offered.

    What comes back

    :results is read the way org reads it, and what is not said is guessed at from the output rather than assumed:

    Written Means
    :results output What it printed
    :results value What it returned - python is wrapped in a function
    :results table Read the output as a table
    :results list Each line an item
    :results file The output is a filename; comes back as a link
    :results raw As it stands
    nothing Output, and a table if it looks like one

    "Looks like one" is three shapes: lines already written as an org table, lines separated by tabs, and the list of lists a python or lisp block prints when it returns one. Anything else is text, because a paragraph split into columns on a guess is worse than a paragraph.

    Table Browsing And Editing

    The table endpoints let a client list every org table the server knows about and edit one as a spreadsheet. A table is addressed by the file it lives in plus its ordinal position within that file (Id), counted in document order starting at zero.

    Writing a table only rewrites the lines the table occupies, so the rest of the file is left byte for byte as it was. The #+TBLFM: lines of a table are rewritten as a single line holding every formula, separated by ::.
